Implementation for the Real World
abs: Work on the crucial subject of policy and program implementation was once a central preoccupation among scholars and students of public affairs and public policy. Today it remains so—despite first-glance assessments that interest in the subject may have declined. Indeed, the relevant studies during the past decade or so number well over a thousand (Moulton, Roll, and Sandfort forthcoming; Saetren 2014). A journal, Implementation Science, was founded in 2006, although its narrow jurisdiction (“routine healthcare”) and relative neglect of the broader implementation universe sometimes seems to signal a reinvention of the proverbial wheel, albeit in an important domain. Much of the relevant recent research, unfortunately for those interested in general implementation theory and practice, is published in policy sector-specific outlets. The book-length studies that remain of general interest are mostly older and, in important respects, unreflective of recent research developments. As a consequence, current general texts are in short supply. Implementation has traveled a circuitous route from its origins as a self-aware subject to its status as a mature and nuanced theme today. Despite the twists and turns of academic and research fashion, nonetheless, the practical challenges of effective policy implementation loom, if anything, larger than ever. From the complex and contentious issues of immigration and domestic security to health care and from executing sensible approaches to managing climate change to implementing social programs aimed at improving the lives of millions, policy activists and others stand more than ever in need of sound approaches for converting policy intentions into stable and reliable streams of efficacious public action. The topic as a research subject is potentially overwhelming. As has been widely recognized, dozens of variables are potentially relevant to implementation action; theoretical disputes remain important; and the challenges of validating findings are real, given measurement issues and the heavy albeit not exclusive reliance on case studies and qualitative work. Even so, most of the study of policy implementation is, in a sense, truncated: it is framed through the lens of public policy itself and relatively light on other areas of relevant expertise, including (for instance) behavioral economics. A truly comprehensive volume on implementation would need to push beyond the boundaries of disciplinary specialties. On this issue, the ambitions of Sandfort and Moulton are readily apparent. Their goal is to “integrate considerable research in public policy, economics, sociology, public administration, design, medicine, political science, social work, urban planning, education, and public health” (page xiv); and they draw from all these fields in the course of their exposition. Indeed, although the purpose of the book is explicitly pragmatic, research literatures are certainly not ignored; the volume contains 91 pages of notes and references. That is not to say that they have swept all relevant fields of learning into their approach and integrated them tightly and seamlessly in the service of a full understanding of the subject. For one thing, even more literatures are relevant—take, for instance, the burgeoning research on public management and performance, including now many large-N studies. And for another, as explained more carefully below, this volume provides less than a fully integrated theoretical approach—in fact, it would be difficult to imagine what a full integration would actually look like. Even if Sandfort and Moulton had in mind an approach that would involve a (mere) expansion and updating of many of the relevant research findings into an internally consistent perspective, their volume would be welcome. But—again—their reach extends much further. Unlike the vast majority of scholarly treatments of implementation, this one has Effective Implementation in Practice consistently at the center of the discussion. Their primary interest is in equipping individuals to “mak[e] change in complex systems” (page xiv) toward the purposive creation of public value. It would be difficult to overemphasize how distinctive this aim is. Virtually all book-length treatments of the broad subject of implementation have been written primarily from the perspective of research: how can or should the best implementation research be conducted? What findings have been educed? What theories offer the best prospects for explaining the variance in observed implementation outcomes across cases or contexts or programs? Can a particular framework or theory sketched by the author(s) provide a compelling overall account of the implementation process? While skeptics about the possibility of general theory on the subject can be found (famously, Bardach 1977), most implementation researchers are seekers after this holy grail, and most have in mind other researchers as the main critical audience—despite occasional mentions about shaping “practice” (Goggin et al. 1990). To put the matter another way, the subject of improving practice, treated as the primary focus of the subject of implementation, has mostly been ignored by the research community (O’Toole 2004). Long ago Elmore accused scholars of developing practical injunctions that were “desultory and strategically vague” (1979–1980: 601), and the situation has not been much improved in subsequent years. In this respect, the volume written by Sandfort and Moulton is very different. It puts the world of practice consistently in the foreground. In particular, the authors intend to provide advice for effecting change, since that is the common intent of virtually all new policies and programs. Accordingly, and distinctively, an entire chapter is devoted to the subject of learning in implementation systems, a subject rarely addressed in the implementation literature. The book is designed to highlight the complicated real world and, according to the authors, how practitioners should analyze their situations and address them so as to increase prospects for success. Of course, there are different sorts of practitioners, and they inhabit different niches in the multilevel systems of the policy world. Accordingly, and also distinctively in terms of the literature, Sandfort and Moulton focus on how to assist implementation in practice from multiple strata of the system. In doing so, they move “across schools of thought and units of analysis without getting bogged down in any one particular way of thinking” (pages 35–36). This approach is, accordingly, an unusually far-reaching one. The result is a rather elaborate, and considerably elaborated, perspective grounded on the notion of “strategic action fields” (page 17)—“settings where collective action takes place; participants working together [there] have a general understanding about their purpose, their relationships, and the spoken and unspoken rules that guide their actions” (page 69). Such settings are important at three different “levels:” the policy field (“bounded networks among organizations carrying our a substantive policy and program area in a particular place”), the organization (“authorizing and service organizations that devise the program rules and structure”), and the front lines (“workers or interfaces that directly interact with the target population to carry out the program”) (page 24). Each of these receives a full chapter’s treatment. Action at these levels consists of particular kinds of work and functions to seek accomplishment of a key role. And effective implementation, they argue, is “more akin to gardening than engineering or architecture” (page xiv). Accordingly, at its core effective implementation involves adjusting to unpredictability and tapping creativity more than using any cookbook or even narrowly scientific expertise. This broad framework represents the beginning rather than the completion of the conceptual development. And at every stage of analysis throughout the book, two public programs are used to anchor the explication and offer concrete illustrations of how to conduct implementation analyses. These programs, the Hardest Hit Fund (aimed at addressing the housing foreclosure crisis of the Great Recession) and the Quality Rating and Improvement System (crafted to improve early education settings), tap expertise of Moulton and Sandfort, respectively. The result is a rich, multidisciplinary, and unusually grounded treatment of the complex terrain. The challenges and limitations of seeking to draw together multiple theoretical lines of analysis, not to mention levels of analysis, echo in a sense the realism but also the limitations of bottom-up analyses from yesteryear: the theoretical logic can tend to sacrifice parsimony—and also potential predictive power—for more comprehensiveness. Top-downers have criticized bottom-uppers for emphasizing the context-specific and complicated nature of implementation, at the expense of theoretical leverage. (Bottom-uppers, on the other hand, would often appropriately fault top-down analysis for its lack of realism and implicit obeisance to the criterion of compliance at the expense of problem solving.) Sandfort and Moulton seek to bridge the twin poles of theoretical complexity and oversimplification, and their work takes us far beyond the injunction that the policy world is complicated and difficult to design. In particular, their parsing of different levels into distinct strategic action fields implies helpful differentiation of partial theories and discipline-based heuristics into spheres where they can be most sensibly applied. As analysts have long observed, theoretical explanations vary widely between macro- and micro-dynamics of implementation, with different causal arguments operating at these different levels (multilevel analytical techniques have generally not been invoked to study implementation). In this book, Sandfort and Moulton explicitly acknowledge the very different kinds of explanations needed at different levels of a complex policy system by incorporating three of them, without carefully and explicitly mapping the details of the causal processes of each onto the others. An obvious result is that the approach does not tie together all the loose theoretical ends in the extant literature—nor could one reasonably expect it to. This choice seems especially apropos given the purpose of the book: to serve as a text for those planning or engaged in professional practice, rather than those seeking primarily to move research frontiers on policy implementation forward. After all, we do not encounter the rich real world as a straightforward linear logic, as on a course syllabus or in a deductively generated research agenda; rather, we apprehend it as a pastiche of partially analyzable and partially discordant subsets. This book aims to sketch the terrain of policy implementation and provide approaches to serve as guideposts, replete with immediately practical tools to assist with the kinds of cues and decisions that, if attended to, can add a measure of efficacy to the efforts to convert policy intention into desired results—as seen by any of those whose aim is to solve a practical challenge as embedded in public policy, whether policy designers or program managers or front-line policy workers or stakeholders in the ultimate products of policy-relevant action. Sandfort and Moulton do much more than hint at or allude to the relevant heuristics. At several of the concrete steps of their analysis, they develop an explicit link to a document or interview protocol or decision template to assist readers in taking those steps with specific reference to a policy problem or program the reader may be grappling with. Eight of these practical aids comprise the Appendices to the text coverage. Still, the theoretical argument is far from succinct. Meier (1999) once irreverently suggested that any implementation scholar who desired to introduce a new variable to account for program outputs and outcomes should be required to propose the elimination of two extant variables in prevailing theoretical arguments. That exchange has clearly not happened within the pages of Effective Implementation in Practice. The contributions represented in this book, nonetheless, are substantial. Still, as the authors would surely agree, the arguments presented are not the final word on the subject. Further theoretical development, for instance on the specification of links across levels, would be welcome. Coverage is implicitly focused on the United States, and of course practical requirements and opportunities vary considerably across national settings—not to mention the important challenge of implementing international agreements—thus suggesting even more relevant levels of analysis. And it would be useful to know which of the numerous heuristics offered here may be more important and which able to be sacrificed when time or resources are scarce. But these points do not suggest serious problems with the current volume; rather, they indicate a few of the directions available for further development. Sandfort and Moulton have done an unusual service to the community of implementation scholars and—rarely and especially—practitioners. This provocative and valuable book should be studied carefully by all who are serious about the promise and perils of implementation.

t: The Impact of Empathy—Explaining Diversity in Street-Level Decision-Making
abs: This article investigates whether the empathic abilities of street-level bureaucrats have an impact on their discretionary decision-making. The impact of empathic abilities on decision-making is considered an important research question, as our knowledge remains limited as to the importance of personal ability on decisions. The article further contributes to the field of street-level bureaucracy by conducting a discrete choice experiment, an approach highly suitable for examining discretionary decision-making. The article draws on nationally representative survey data from 268 employees in correctional facilities in Denmark, with a 67.5% response rate. The findings confirm that discretionary decision-making is affected by the empathic abilities of bureaucrats. However, the impact of empathy depends on the severity of inmates’ infringement against the rules. In essence, the findings demonstrate that personal abilities may advantageously be incorporated into further studies as an important determinant of street-level behavior. Der Beitrag untersucht, inwieweit die empathischen Fähigkeiten von "Street-Level-Bürokraten“ einen Einfluss auf deren Ermessensentscheidungen haben. Dies ist eine relevante Forschungsfrage, da relativ wenig über den Effekt von persönlichen Eigenschaften auf das Entscheidungsverhalten bekannt ist. Der Artikel leistet ebenfalls einen Beitrag zur Forschung im Bereich der Street-Level-Bureaucracy, indem er ein Discrete-Choice-Experiment durchführt; eine geeignete Methode zum Erforschen von Ermessenspielräumen. Der Beitrag basiert auf national-repräsentativen Survey-Daten von 268 Mitarbeitern aus der Strafvollzugsverwaltung Dänemarks (Rücklaufquote: 67,5%). Die Ergebnisse belegen, dass empathische Fähigkeiten einen Einfluss auf das Ausschöpfen von Ermessenspielräumen haben. Allerdings ist das Maß an Empathie von der Schwere der Regelverstöße der Insassen abhängig. Insgesamt deuten die Ergebnisse darauf hin, dass zukünftige Studien persönliche Fähigkeiten als wichtige Determinanten des Verhaltens der Street-Level-Verwaltung berücksichtigen sollten. t: When Ties Bind: Public Managers’ Networking Behavior and Municipal Fiscal Health After the Great Recession
abs: This study examines the relationship between managerial networking and the fiscal health of city governments in the United States that faced a serious budget crisis during and immediately after the Great Recession. Do public managers’ ties with external stakeholders help improve the fiscal health of these cities? Or do these ties bind city officials to decisions that further exacerbate the fiscal difficulties of their governments? These questions are answered using data from a survey of municipal governments across the United States with a population of 50,000 or more, and financial data from Comprehensive Annual Financial Reports (CAFR) covering more than 200 cities and for three fiscal years. Using instrumental variable regression to address possible common source bias and simultaneous causation, there is strong evidence that an external networking orientation is associated with a decline in city government fiscal health, whether the measure used is perceptual or CAFR-based. Der Beitrag untersucht die Beziehung des Networkings von Managern und der fiskalischen Verfassung von Stadtverwaltungen in den Vereinigten Staaten, die sich mit einem Haushaltsnotstand im Zuge der letzten Weltwirtschaftskrise konfrontiert sahen. Helfen die Netzwerke von Führungskräften in der Verwaltung, die Finanzprobleme dieser Städte zu überwinden? Oder binden diese Netzwerke die Verwaltung an Entscheidungen, die die Haushaltsprobleme weiter verschärfen? Diese Fragen werden mittels Daten eines Surveys von Kommunalverwaltungen in den Vereinigten Staaten mit mehr als 50.000 Einwohnern sowie Finanzstatistiken (Annual Financial Reports), die mehr als 200 Städte über drei Jahre hinweg erfassen, beantwortet. Basierend auf Regressionen mit instrumentellen Variablen, die Methodenbias- und Kausalitäts-Probleme adressieren, finden wir einschlägige Belege dafür, dass externes Networking mit fiskalischen Problemen assoziiert ist, unabhängig davon, ob Einschätzungen oder Finanzstatistiken als Messgrundlage benutzt werden. t: The Ins and Outs of PerformanceStat
abs: Performance management has been around for a while. As research on the subject accumulated, we began to throw some basic assumptions overboard. No, performance information is not more objective than, or superior to, other feedback. It will not revolutionize decision-making or make it more rational; rather, existing routines and mental models shape the role of performance information in organizations. We also know that performance data use is often biased, political, and driven by self-interest. Despite our progress on the research front, we are still struggling with some major questions: Does performance management work? We have been answering this question, stating that “it depends.” But what does it depend on? How does context matter? And which contingencies do we need to be aware of? How can we make people care about performance information? It is not uncommon that a great deal of resources is devoted to measurement efforts, while managers disregard data when making decisions. At the same time, how can we make sure that people do not “care” so much about performance data that they are tempted to falsify and game them in order to receive bonuses or escape punishment and blame? While reading Robert Behn’s book I was curious to see if his PerformanceStat approach could provide new insights into these issues. More and more public organizations have adopted performance systems that are loosely based on the same principles and use the suffix Stat in their name. The first one was CompStat, developed by the police in New York City (NYPD) and adopted by other police departments. This was followed by Baltimore’s citywide adaptation CitiStat and variations of AgencyStat and JurisdictionStat. Behn refers to the entire category as PerformanceStat which includes, among others, ParkStat, JobStat, ChildStat, PhillyStat, and StateStat (chapters 1 and 2). But what is so special about the PerformanceStat approach that it spread across agencies, jurisdictions, levels of government, and is being used beyond the United States? How is it different from performance management as we know it? Generally, performance management is about measuring the status quo, defining future objectives, and closing gaps between performance aspirations and reality. It requires the use of indicators, targets, and performance information as well as the establishment of data collection, analysis, and use routines (Van Dooren, Bouckaert, and Halligan 2015). To me, three features stand out that make the PerformanceStat approach unique: leadership involvement, meeting format, and data characteristics. While conventional performance management efforts have, at times, been criticized to turn into compliance exercises with little top-level interest, PerformanceStat requires leaders not only to be committed but also to be involved (chapter 16). Here, it is the leadership team who runs the Stat meetings on a regular basis. In these meetings, performance data are shown on big screens, and the leadership team interviews middle managers, one at a time, about their unit’s performance deficits and initiatives to resolve them (chapter 10). There is persistent follow-up between meetings. At the beginning of each one, middle managers use data to report on the success of past initiatives and explain progress or obstacles (chapter 11). In order to be able to assess possible improvements between meetings, indicators need to be sensitive to short-term changes and data need to be current. This is why PerformanceStat requires leaders to look at disaggregated data beyond a handful of big picture outcomes that conventional performance management practices often call for (chapter 8). Behn’s holistic conceptualization of PerformanceStat includes more than the three features that I identified as most unique (chapter 3). He blends them with known good-practice prescriptions which would most likely help improve any type of performance management, not just PerformanceStat. Leaders need to commit to a specific purpose they want to achieve, identify performance deficits, and set targets (chapter 5). They need to delegate responsibility and discretion for improving performance to middle managers and their subunits (chapter 6). Leaders (as well as managers and analysts) need to search for patterns in their data, identify reference points, and ask the right questions (chapter 9). They need to learn how to use data to sort out the best ways to meet targets but also how to reinvent and adapt PerformanceStat after the first generation of performance issues has been resolved (chapter 13). Leaders also need to support the development of performance management-related human competencies in their organizations (chapter 12). Behn argues that PerformanceStat is an integrated leadership strategy. Only if leaders pay equal attention to all the aspects of the improvement effort will they be able to exploit the full PerformanceStat potential. Behn refrains from using the term “system” when describing PerformanceStat because he doesn’t want to imply that improvements occur automatically once some system components have been adopted (e.g., computer screens in meeting rooms, data dashboards on Web sites, live streams of the Stat meetings). Instead, he argues that PerformanceStat needs to be adapted to specific contexts, not copied. Leaders need to be engaged in its implementation, rather than just adopt a trendy toolkit (“MimicStat,” p. 230ff.), without putting it to purposeful use. Now let us return to my questions from the beginning: Does PerformanceStat work? Behn refers to a quote which states that asking whether CompStat works makes as much sense as asking whether surgery works (p. 57f.). He has a point there, arguing that, just like surgery, CompStat (or PerformanceStat more generally) sometimes works and sometimes doesn’t. Yet, I would argue that just as hospitals have an interest in tracking their average error rates for surgeries, public management scholars and practitioners have an interest in understanding whether (and why), on average, Stat has led to performance improvements or not. Of course, Behn doesn’t leave it at this and devotes two full chapters to the issue. He reviews research on CompStat and crime, concluding that there are at least 10 credible reasons to explain why crime has gone down, and CompStat is only one of them (chapter 4). He also zooms in on four cases (New Orleans, Los Angeles County, Washington, DC, and Baltimore) and shows that the use of PerformanceStat approaches has helped better deal with blight, potholes, homeless shelters, and DNA samples (chapter 7). I agree with Behn that proofing the PerformanceStat effect is difficult. Stat can mean different things in different places, the use of Stat may overlap with other variables, and we are unable to study this using randomized experiments. However, if we cannot say with some certainty that PerformanceStat is likely to improve results, then discussions about how and why to employ this approach can easily be rendered pointless. Where does this leave us as researchers? Well, policy areas in which the same performance data were tracked before and after the adoption of PerformanceStat, and in which some organizations opted for the adoption while others did not, constitute quasi-experiments. So, for example, we could compare the performance differences between matched adopters and non-adopters while accounting for pre-adoption performance scores and other confounding factors. We could also use Behn’s conceptualization to measure how organizations score on a PerformanceStat index to sort out the apples-and-oranges problem when comparing Stat approaches. If PerformanceStat sometimes works, what is this dependent on, and how do context and contingencies matter? Behn does consider moderating factors. One of his main points is, in fact, that the adoption of the structural features of PerformanceStat will only lead to improvements if this is complemented by the implementation of related leadership behaviors (see chapters 14 and 15). He also makes the case that it is easier to implement PerformanceStat in some contexts than in others, which makes this approach more likely to succeed under certain circumstances. This is mainly due to data availability, the visibility of outputs, and the presence of similar subunits which may serve as reference groups. Hence, the police has an advantage, production organizations have it easier than coping organizations, and agencies have an advantage over jurisdictions. We could speculate about other contingency factors which are not considered in the book. Does PerformanceStat work better in contexts in which almost everything is messed up—that is, where one starts off with massive performance deficits? Here, support for more aggressive accountability approaches would be high, and low-hanging “performance fruits” numerous. Some of the most famous PerformanceStat cases (the NYPD and Baltimore) used to be in this category. What about the role of organizational culture? A hierarchical culture might mitigate the PerformanceStat effect, but a rational culture could enhance it. The moderating impact of a group or a developmental culture may, in turn, be dependent on the way PerformanceStat is being implemented (“the brutal” vs. “the bland,” p. 178ff.). How can we make people care about performance information, while simultaneously not allowing data to corrupt people’s behavior? PerformanceStat establishes routines of data review and follow-up which make managers discuss performance information and, ideally, learn from positive deviants. Its transparency also puts pressure on managers to know their numbers, be able to explain them, and take actions to achieve targets in order to maintain their professional reputation and look good in front of peers. The book addresses the NYPD’s downgrading of crime which has been associated with CompStat, but it does not investigate cheating and gaming as a more systemic issue (Eterno and Silverman 2012). We know that performance indicators can corrupt behavior, particularly when tasks are complex and pressure high or rewards substantial. In such cases, measured performance is at risk of being improved through goal displacement or data manipulation, rather than actual efficiency or effectiveness gains (Kroll and Moynihan 2015). PerformanceStat in its more aggressive configuration can create such a high pressure environment. Behn does warn that pressure may be useful to better exploit existing knowledge and resources, but it may also harm innovation and trial-and-error learning needed to explore new ways to achieve the organization’s mission. The book is based on dozens of Stat cases but mainly draws on success stories as illustrative examples. To generate more insights into the dysfunctions of PerformanceStat (the psychology behind them and possible remedies), the book could have also explored one “worst case” or the specific pathologies of an otherwise popular case in greater detail. Behn has written an important book on of one of the “hot topics” of performance management. My remarks point to avenues for further discussion and research, rather than to substantial deficiencies of the book. It is certainly not a step-by-step manual on how to implement PerformanceStat, and I would have been worried if it had tried to be that. Instead, Behn emphasizes the need to adapt PerformanceStat applications to different contexts throughout his book, while providing nuanced guidance based on behavioral theory and his case illustrations. “The PerformanceStat Potential” surely has its place in our graduate classes on performance management. For instructors with little room to expand their syllabi, I recommend taking a closer look at chapters 3, 10, and 15 (definitions, meetings, and leadership behaviors) which provide a good overview of both: the uniqueness of the approach as well as the need to implement it as an integrated leadership strategy. The book is a must-read for managers who consider adopting PerformanceStat in their organizations as well as managers who have already adopted a “SomethingStat system” but are perplexed that it hasn’t produced the expected results. Behn’s writing and sense of humor make the book a pleasant read.

t: The Incompetence Trap: The (Conditional) Irrelevance of Agency Expertise
abs: Formal models of the appointments process typically cast the decision of the appointing executive as one where an open position is assumed and an appointee is chosen in order to maximize the utility of the executive (and perhaps that of the legislature if confirmation is required). However, several—often patronage-focused—processes within the appointments process focus instead on finding acceptable positions for “necessary-to-place” individuals. Here, I develop a model where the goal is to find the best position for such an individual. In contrast to many existing models of the appointments process, I find that when the personnel process is focused on finding the best position for a given person as opposed to finding the best person for a given position, “turkey farms”—agencies that have high numbers of minimally-competent (but necessary-to-place) individuals among their ranks—can result in equilibrium. Moreover, once agency capacity is sufficiently low, incompetent individual appointees no longer have detrimental effects on the utilities of the appointing principals, which further incentivizes the usage of certain agencies as “turkey farms.”

t: The Twentieth-Century Administrative State and Networked Governance
abs: Since its founding, the American state has relied both upon what we now call “traditional” administration—public, hierarchical, and bureaucratic—and upon more privatized approaches to governance involving state and non-state actors and institutions in contractual relationships and networks. Studying past public–private governance schemes affords new opportunities to understand why, how, and under what circumstances state actors eschew direct public action in favor of boundary-spanning arrangements. I demonstrate this by presenting a case study of the National Defense Research Committee (NDRC), a new Federal entity created in 1940 by President Franklin Roosevelt. NDRC relied upon contracting and an existing scientific community to create a highly effective network of scientists and laboratories spanning the public, for profit, and nonprofit sectors. Beyond presenting novel empirical evidence, I contribute to theory by providing new insights into the factors and conditions that spur state actors to adopt a networked approach to governance, and by proposing the concept of a “twilight” network, defined as a network whose structure and behavior are legal, yet simultaneously overt and covert. I also show that qualitative, detailed historical research may valuably extend our understanding of public–private governance arrangements and the “state of agents.” Seit seiner Gründung beruht der amerikanische Staat sowohl auf "traditioneller“ Verwaltung (öffentlich, hierarchisch, bürokratisch) als auch auf privatisierten Formen des Regierens, die Regierungs- und Nichtregierungs-Akteure und Institutionen mittels vertraglicher Beziehungen und Netzwerke einbinden. Das Erforschen von historischen öffentlich-privaten Regierungsmodellen eröffnet neue Möglichkeiten, besser zu verstehen, warum, inwieweit und unter welchen Bedingungen Verwaltungen sektorübergreifende Arrangements gegenüber klassischen öffentlichen Initiativen bevorzugen. Ich untersuche dies mittels einer Fallstudie des Nationalen Komitees für Verteidigungsforschung (NDRC), das von Präsident Roosevelt ins Leben gerufen wurde und während des zweiten Weltkriegs aktiv war. Das NDRC gründete sich auf eine existierende Forschungsgemeinschaft und nutzte Verträge und Leistungsvereinbarungen, um ein hoch effektives sektorübergreifendes Netzwerk von Wissenschaftlern und Laboren zu schaffen. Zusätzlich zu diesem empirischen Beitrag trägt der Artikel zur Theoriebildung bei, indem er neue Erkenntnisse über Faktoren gewinnt, die die Bildung von Netzwerken befördern. Ich entwickle ebenfalls das Konzept des "Twilight“-Netzwerks, definiert als Netzwerk, dessen Struktur und Verhalten legal ist, welches allerdings auch als offen und gleichzeitig als versteckt charakterisiert werden kann. Ich zeige zudem, dass qualitative, detaillierte historische Forschung unser Verständnis von öffentlich-privaten Regierungsarrangements sowie vom Gewährleistungsstaat verbessert. t: How Do Politicians Attribute Bureaucratic Responsibility for Performance? Negativity Bias and Interest Group Advocacy
abs: Voters reward or punish politicians by deeming them responsible for positive and negative outcomes, but how, in turn, do politicians attribute responsibility to those who actually deliver public services? Inattention to this question renders incomplete current perspectives on democratic processes of accountability, even as politicians are increasingly provided with performance data to hold bureaucrats accountable. We shed light on this issue using a survey experiment of elected officials featuring actual performance data. We find that the provision of performance data makes elected officials more willing to attribute causal responsibility to bureaucratic leaders, but only in cases of low performance, suggesting a negativity bias in public sector responsibility attribution processes. Additionally, we offer evidence that interest group advocates influence how elected officials use performance information to attribute responsibility, but contingent on ideological alignment.

t: Voices from the Frontline: Network Participation and Local Support for National Policy Reforms
abs: In this article, I explore the determinants of frontline service organizations’ support for and implementation of social policy reforms in the context of the US national health care reform. Ascribing to theories of inter-organizational collaboration, I argue that local service organizations, as the frontline agents of policy changes, develop their policy preferences and implementation activities in accordance with the collaborative networks, in which they situated. Network participation reduces uncertainty about the new political environment and motivates organizations to join the reform coalition. Using a sample of near 1,000 American hospitals, I offer the first systematic study of hospital chief administrators’ support for the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA), as well as their hospitals’ preparation for and compliance with the ACA. I find hospital managers who actively engage in external networking activities are more likely to support increasing government role in providing health care insurance. Hospitals that actively participate in service collaboration are also more likely to comply with the ACA. These findings challenge the conventional view of frontline service organizations that they passively adapt to political changes. This article also adds to the network collaboration literature by showing that networking activities not only affect organizational performance, but also shape organizations’ preferences about government solutions to social problems.

t: Maybe It Is Time to Rediscover Technocracy? An Old Framework for a New Analysis of Administrative Reforms in the Governance Era
abs: The article argues that recent decades of administrative policy and reform have led to the emergence of a late modern technocracy, defined by the intersecting ideas and principles of connective governance, risk management, and performance management. Connectivity, risk, and performance have remained consistent concerns across the various market-based and/or network-based alternatives to bureaucracy found in New Public Management (NPM) and post-NPM reforms. In contrast to the image of a flexible compromise between bureaucracy, markets, and networks prevailing in current debate, the article suggests that the long-standing tension between technocracy and bureaucracy are of vital importance to the administrations of advanced liberal democracies. Indeed, the partial compromise between technocracy and bureaucracy reached in the earlier creation of a “techno-bureaucracy” designed for planning and social engineering has been largely supplanted by a more adversarial stance towards bureaucracy in late modern technocracy due to the requirements of connectivity, risk, and performance. Der Beitrag argumentiert, dass Verwaltungspolitiken und -reformen in den letzten Jahrzehnten zu der Herausbildung einer späten modernen Technokratie geführt haben, definiert durch überschneidende Ideen und Prinzipien wie Vernetzte Verwaltung, Risiko-Management und Performance Management. Digitalisierung, Risiko und Performance sind aktuelle Themen in verschiedenen "New Public Management (NPM)“-Reformen und Post-NPM-Ansätzen, die Alternativen zur klassischen Bürokratie darstellen. Im Gegensatz zu dem Leitbild des flexiblen Kompromisses zwischen Bürokratie, Märkten und Netzwerken, das die derzeitige Debatte beherrscht, verweist dieser Beitrag auf die anhaltende Spannung zwischen Technokratie und Bürokratie und deren Bedeutung für die Verwaltung in entwickelten, liberalen Demokratien. Der partielle Kompromiss zwischen Technokratie und Bürokratie, der zur Schaffung der "Techno-Bürokratie“ führte, deren Fokus vor allem auf der Planung und dem "Social Engineering“ lag, wurde weitestgehend durch eine kritische Perspektive gegenüber der Bürokratie und durch einen neuen Fokus auf Digitalisierung, Risiko und Performance abgelöst. t: Navigating Scarcity: Can Nongovernmental Institutions Address US Organ Donor Needs?
abs: The question of how to regulate, facilitate, and prioritize scarce cadaveric organs for patients in need, many of whom are in dire life and death situations, has all of the makings of a high-drama policy puzzle. Specifically, the emotionally laden nature of the question itself as well as significant challenges to attaining efficiency without violating ethical standards, make coordinating organ procurement and transplantation a particular challenge. The expansive geography of the United States and the various interests that influence (or seek to influence) decision-making in this domain further complicate these discussions. In this deeply researched and eminently readable book, David L. Weimer offers not only a fresh look at the particular institutional arrangements developed to address this problem—that of turning to the private rulemaking body known as the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN)—but also asks the larger question of whether the establishment of similar private rulemaking bodies might hold promise for solving other vexing policy puzzles. Weimer’s central interest is the potential that private rulemaking bodies may or may not hold. He describes these bodies as an “arrangement in which stakeholders exercise explicitly delegated authority over the development and adoption of rules within the framework of a nongovernmental organization, or in the terminology of network theory, a network administrative organization” (1). In making his argument in favor of at least considering the potential that such institutional arrangements might have beyond OPTN, Weimer walks readers through some of the issues that OPTN previously faced. For example, Chapter 2 evaluates trade-offs in governance as they arise with respect to values, expertise, and interests. Five subsequent chapters explore, with great detail, the OPTN itself and the various challenges it has had to overcome. Chapter 3 provides an overview of OPTN’s genesis and its interactions with the federal government, especially the Department of Health and Human Services. This chapter, on its own, would prove useful for teaching purposes in situations where time does not allow for a more extensive consideration of the policy challenges of organ procurement, but instructors are looking for a way to draw out the differences between, for example, OPTN and the Food and Drug Administration, perhaps to draw contrasts between what Daniel Carpenter (2010) describes in his book on the FDA and alternative regulatory approaches. Chapter 4 casts challenges associated with organ supply as questions of governance and articulates differences in cadaveric and live-donor organs. Chapter 5 examines controversies in OPTN rule formation for liver donation and allocation, especially as policy has moved away from local boundaries and toward regional allocation. Here, Weimer shows the delicate balance that groups, such as the OPTN, must play in managing both internal and external perceptions, a point that will remind some readers of Carpenter’s emphasis on “reputation” as an institutional concern. Chapter 6 examines controversies in racial disparity in kidney allocation, showing how OPTN used incremental rulemaking to reduce disparities across a 15-year time span. Chapter 7 considers the potential of private rulemaking bodies such as OPTN to bring about noticeable change, using OPTN’s lung allocation system as a case study. Chapters 8 and 9 fill out the theoretical bases of OPTN-like institutions, explaining why, in Weimer’s view, private rule making bodies hold promise for superior evidence-based rule making, at least in some policy domains. Although Medical Governance’s substantive focus is organ transplantation, its scholarly contribution primarily concerns the question of private rulemaking. It will therefore be of great interest not only to those interested in the ethics and logistics of organ donation, but as a means of exploring the potential of private rulemaking to consider other policy domains that might benefit from such an approach. Weimer limits his exploration of this potential primarily to challenges in the health sector, such as the need to produce an effective electronic medical records system linked more assuredly to medical evidence as well as the need to devise better strategies for allocating surgical resources. Despite challenges, Weimer makes a persuasive case that policymakers should at least consider the possibility that the establishment of provide bodies that interact with federal agencies might hold promise given the eight values of private rulemaking bodies he identifies: professional engagement, continuity, meaningful stakes, decision making by voting, specialization with consultation, transparency, data for creating evidence, and strategic oversight. Though Weimer sees potential in the extension of OPTN-like institutions as a general policy tool, he acknowledges that his study is limited in its capacity to say with certainty how radical that potential may be. This is because, as he acknowledges at several points, he turned to the question of organ procurement and allotment with regard to private rulemaking precisely because OPTN is “an unusual institution of medical governance” (167)—indeed, perhaps the only one that fits the bill of a major policy question in which rulemaking is delegated to nongovernmental stakeholders. Nonetheless, Weimer believes that his consideration of other policy questions suggests, at a minimum, “the potential for greater use of private rulemaking in medical governance” (167). Weimer may be right. But Medical Governance also makes clear that the OPTN is not merely the only example we have of such an approach to rulemaking; it owes instead to a particular history as well as the uniqueness of the question of organ procurement itself. In the domain of policy regarding both live-donor and cadaveric organs, OPTN seems to have come a long way and been recognized by the federal government as worthy of retaining, and even primed to capitalize on its existing structure, precisely because there was already in place a network of stakeholders that had developed. In other words, the history that Weimer provides, which is a useful and real contribution to the scholarship in and of itself, raises the question of whether OPTN is more unique and more exceptional than he acknowledges, even to such a point that it undercuts, at least to some degree, his argument that similar bodies could mold themselves in OPTN’s image. I raise this not as a criticism of Weimer’s text, but in the interest of underscoring the extent to which Weimer’s portrayal of OPTN will help readers to appreciate just how interesting OPTN’s history is, which will similarly impress upon readers the extent to which organ procurement and allotment is hard to compare to other policy questions precisely because of its emotional and unique economic and ethical dimensions. With these limitations in mind, the importance of this work lies in Weimer’s focus on modes of rulemaking and oversight, not solving problems associated with organ procurement and allotment as such, despite gains that have been made. Perhaps most obvious on this score is the fact that Weimer is not concerned in this text with advancing strategies for increasing the stock of cadaveric organs. Instead, with his focus on the theory of governance within OPTN-like institutions, Weimer largely takes the world as it is instead of how it could be. Weimer’s text proceeds from an assumption that scarcity is something of a fact instead of a function of political culture or policy decisions. Indeed, many countries have sought to reduce (though not eliminate) scarcity by flipping on its head the United States’ “opt-in” approach to donation in which individuals must specifically elect to donate their organs in the event of death. Specifically, 24 European countries, and many countries around the world, have developed opt-out systems in which consent to donate is presumed unless otherwise stated. This policy switch has drastically increased these countries’ stock of cadaveric organs. For Weimer’s interest in governance issues, it is notable that organ donation in Europe is overseen not by a private rulemaking body but is regulated by formal governmental bodies. And though increasing the stock of cadaveric organs through the establishment of an opt-out systems does not, on its own, solve distribution questions, reducing scarcity certainly helps relieve many pressure points that beset the American approach. Again, I raise this not as a criticism of Weimer, for whom such questions are not his focus, but instead to remind those interested in the kind of questions that Medical Governance addresses. Specifically relevant is that institutional efficiency and effectiveness can benefit from a sustained engagement with foundational questions as well, beyond how institutions are structured. Accordingly, with regard to Weimer’s interest in electronic medical records and resources for surgery, it is important to keep in mind that most policy challenges are as much a function of cultural and political–economic hurdles as they are questions of institutional organization and governance.

t: A Matter of Trust: Street Level Bureaucrats, Organizational Climate and Performance Management Reform
abs: The effects of performance management—on organizational outcomes and, to a lesser extent, organizational behavior—have been widely studied. However, we know little about how organizations dominated by street-level bureaucrats respond to performance management reform. Focusing on one large urban school district that adopted performance management reforms in 2007, this article analyzes qualitative and quantitative data to understand how organizational climate shapes street-level bureaucrats’ performance management values and performance management behavior. Using a validated scale of organizational climate, it finds that a human relations climate is positively associated with the espousal performance management values and performance management behaviors. Individual dimensions of human relations climate, moreover, exhibit different effects. A climate that prioritizes employee welfare is positively associated with performance management reform, while one that facilitates employee involvement and dissent is negatively associated with performance management reform. Moreover, certain elements of climate, such as trust among colleagues and supervisory support, affect certain performance behaviors more than others. Die Wirkungen von Performance Management auf Verhalten und Outcomes von Organisationen sind bereits umfassend erforscht. Allerdings ist wesentlich weniger darüber bekannt, inwieweit Organisationen, die von "Street-Level-Bürokraten“ dominiert werden, zu Performance-Management-Reformen stehen. Dieser Beitrag untersucht einen großen urbanen Schulbezirk, in dem Performance-Management-Reformen im Jahre 2007 umgesetzt wurden, und analysiert qualitative und quantitative Daten, um besser zu verstehen, inwieweit das organisationale Klima einen Einfluss auf Performance-Management-spezifische Werte und entsprechendes Verhalten von Street-Level- Bürokraten hat. Basierend auf einer validierten Skala zur Messung des Organisationsklimas zeigt der Beitrag, dass ein Human-Relations-Klima positiv mit Performance-Management-spezifischen Werten und Aktivitäten assoziiert ist. Die einzelnen Dimensionen des Human-Relations-Klimas zeigen allerdings differenzierte Effekte. Ein Klima mit einem Fokus auf das Wohl der Mitarbeiter ist positiv mit Performance-Management-Reformen assoziiert, während ein Klima der Mitarbeiterpartizipation und der Meinungsverschiedenheit einen negativen Effekt hat. Außerdem beeinflussen bestimmte Elemente des Klimas, zum Beispiel Vertrauen unter Kollegen und Unterstützung durch die Führungskraft, Performance-orientiertes Verhalten mehr als andere. t: Three Sides of the Same Coin? A Bayesian Analysis of Strategic Management, Comprehensive Planning, and Inclusionary Values in Land Use
abs: Local government managers face fundamental, value conflicts when they engage urban land use issues. Despite the planet’s ongoing urbanization, managerial influence on land use policy remains an under-examined arena. Local governments are routinely asked to balance economic, ecological, and social equity concerns when making choices between alternative land use policy tools. Are local government sustainable development efforts more strategic, comprehensive, and inclusive than when led by professional public managers rather than elected mayors? How do the institutional forms of government inhibit or enhance the ability of specific policy demanders to influence the use of these tools under varying economic conditions? We answer these questions by examining the relationship between local government structure and land use policy utilization in different economic environments with a Bayesian analysis of surveys of Florida cities at three time periods. Differences between manager and mayoral executive leadership shape public management strategies, comprehensiveness, and inclusionary motives linked to land use policy tool utilization before and after the housing boom of the mid-2000s. However, management turnover mitigates this effect. Moreover, managerial influence is not evident at the housing bubble’s peak, which we argue is an important caveat to the empirical evidence on form of government. Kommunalverwaltungen sehen sich fundamentalen Wertekonflikten ausgesetzt, wenn sie sich im Bereich der Raumnutzung engagieren. Trotz einem generellen Trend zur Urbanisierung ist der Einfluss von Verwaltungsmanagern auf die Raumnutzung weitestgehend unerforscht. Kommunalverwaltungen müssen in aller Regel ökonomische, ökologische und soziale Bedürfnisse austarieren, wenn sie zwischen verschiedenen Politikinstrumenten für die Landnutzung wählen. Sind kommunale Nachhaltigkeitspolitiken strategischer, umfassender und inklusiver, wenn sie von professionellen Verwaltungsmanagern oder von gewählten Bürgermeistern gesteuert werden? Welchen Einfluss haben verschiedene institutionelle Regierungsformen auf die Rolle von Interessenvertretern in diesem Prozess, wenn sich die ökonomischen Rahmenbedingungen verändern? Wir beantworten diese Fragen, indem wir die Beziehung zwischen kommunalen Regierungsstrukturen und Raumnutzungspolitiken in verschiedenen ökonomischen Umfeldern mittels einer bayesianischen Analyse von Surveys in Florida zu drei Zeitpunkten untersuchen. Unterschiede zwischen Managern und Bürgermeistern haben einen Einfluss auf Strategien, Umfang und Inklusivität von Raumnutzungspolitiken vor sowie nach dem Immobilienboom zu Beginn des 21. Jahrhunderts. Allerdings haben Fluktuationen auf den Managementpositionen einen abmildernden Effekt. Darüber hinaus hatten Manager keinen Einfluss während der Zeit der Immobilienblase, weshalb wir Vorbehalte bezüglich der empirischen Beweiskraft von Regierungsformen haben. t: Transparency at the Parish Pump: A Field Experiment to Measure the Effectiveness of Freedom of Information Requests in England
abs: How effective are systems of transparency, such as Freedom of Information (FOI) requests? The ambitious aims of FOI laws hinge on whether requests produce the desired information for the citizens or groups that use them. The question is whether such legally mandated requests work better than more informal mechanisms. Despite the high hopes of advocates, organizational routines, lack of awareness or resistance may limit legal access and public bodies may seek to comply minimally rather than behave in concordance with the spirit of the law. This article reports a field experiment that compared FOI requests and informal nonlegal asks to assess which is more effective in accessing information from English parish councils. The basic premise of statutory access is borne out. FOI requests are more effective than simple asks and the size or preexisting level of openness of a body appears to make little difference to their responsiveness. FOI requests are more effective in encouraging bodies to do more than the law asks (concordance) than encouraging more minimal levels of legal cooperation, when a body simply fulfills its obligations to varying degrees (compliance).This finding indicates high levels of support for FOI once it is within the system.

t: Cohering Collaborative Governance
abs: Approximately 25 years ago, Barbara Gray’s Collaborating inspired scholars and practitioners across multiple fields and schools of thought to shift their focus to the study of collaboration. Gray’s effort to map the principles of collaboration and promote it as “a new social norm” (Gray 1989, xv) was perceived by scholars and policy-makers alike as revolutionary. Collaboratives, at that time, were largely perceived as informal, accidental, or at best experimental. Even among its adherents, collaboration was understood as an exception to the rule of hierarchy, a “Plan B” to supplement more traditional forums for problem-solving. Gray’s call to name, organize, and study collaborative enterprises directed researchers and practitioners to expand their vision of policy-making and conflict-management to include these initiatives. In response, scholars across many disciplinary boundaries have explored the use of collaboration, and eventually collaborative governance, both as an elixir to the headaches of hierarchy and as a weapon to eradicate society’s wicked problems. What has emerged is a sea of case studies and meta-analyses that conceptualize collaborative governance, detail its prevalence, isolate its elements, and (attempt to) evaluate its merits. Twenty-five years later, collaborative enterprises are no longer perceived as experimental; collaborative governance is now commonly used in policy arenas across the world. In the United States, for instance, interagency collaboration is regarded as the gold standard (United States Government Accountability Office 2014), and most federal programs require state and local governments to adopt collaborative governance strategies in exchange for federal financial support. However, despite both the prevalence and status of collaborative governance as a method of policy-making, its study remains a loosely integrated field of largely ad hoc (and sometimes conflicting) approaches. Although there is broad agreement about the virtues of collaborative governance as an idea1 and increasing consensus regarding its basic ingredients, we have yet to establish a coherent conception. There is still significant disagreement or variation regarding its defining characteristics, components, and influences. Emerson and Nabatchi’s (2015),Collaborative Governance Regimes quietly but seismically shifts this landscape of potential. As Gray did for the study of collaboration, so too have Emerson and Nabatchi accomplished for the study of collaborative governance. Collaborative Governance Regimes challenges scholars to discipline the study of collaborative governance in order to strengthen its practice. Springboarding from the works of Ansell and Gash (2008), Frederickson (1999, 2007), and Ostrom (2005), among many others, Emerson and Nabatchi catalogue the complexities of collaborative governance while introducing a framework that adds structure and definition. Their “logic model” is both broad enough to accommodate the multiple perspectives, forms, and contexts referenced in collaborative governance scholarship while sufficiently constrained to provide conceptual and empirical rigor. This move toward concretizing collaborative governance—rather than defining it simply as a rejection of hierarchy—acknowledges its significance as a critical and relevant forum for policy-making and “ups the ante” for all future collaborative governance research. Emerson and Nabatchi’s goals are multifaceted. First, as suggested above, they have an interest in disciplining the study of collaborative governance. To further this end, they do not reinvent the wheel. Rather they cull through the abundance of research on collaboration and collaborative enterprises and build, from these independent parts, a portrait of “collaborative governance regimes” (CGR)—which they define as “a type of public governance system in which cross-boundary collaboration represents the predominant mode for conduct, decision-making and activity” (18). In this light, Emerson and Nabatchi’s project offers students of collaborative governance a method for mapping this vast research within a cohesive framework. To be sure, Collaborative Governance Regimes should not be viewed as a textbook on collaborative governance—or a compilation of theoretical and empirical contributions. In their effort to adequately account for the varying scholarly approaches within their model, they necessarily summarize or distill this work. Instead, their contribution is in synthesis, sense-making, articulation, and integration. They amass a wide array of experts and perspectives and nest these contributions within a framework that is both readable and representative. But Emerson and Nabatchi are not content to communicate with an exclusively academic audience. Neither do they limit their data collection to scholarly contributions. Collaborative Governance Regimes is equally engaged with the work and interests of practitioners—those who are engaged in collaborative governance design and implementation. Right alongside their scholarly references appear examples and insights from those who have pioneered best practices in collaborative endeavors in a host of policy realms and regions. For instance, organizational histories, assessment reports, and case studies are integrated within various chapters to provide examples of each element in their model. Additionally, Part III is devoted exclusively to three instances of collaborative governance, each explored in its own chapter and authored by case-specific experts. These chapters provide readers with an empirical illustration to help them understand the practical implications of the model advanced by the authors. In a way, then (like Gray), the book is pitched as a technical guide to, rather than a critique or analysis of, the study and practice of collaborative governance. Scholars are referenced because of the lenses they offer to help illuminate the phenomenon of collaborative governance. Third, Emerson and Nabatchi’s expansive investigation scientifically propels the study of collaborative governance by raising the possibility of species-level analyses. Rather than maintaining a “family-level approach” to studying collaborative governance (and charting the differences between traditional and collaborative decision-making forums), Emerson and Nabatchi develop “a typology that adequately allows for differentiation among the variety of CGR species” (162). Their nod to variation provides a necessary next step in the evolution of collaborative governance scholarship. Unlike past species-level analyses, which were largely only case specific or sector specific (Ansell and Gash, 544) and, therefore, offered little broad-based analytic purchase, Emerson and Nabatchi create a typology of collaborative governance regimes organized around CGR formation. Detailed in Chapter 8, this taxonomy is based on the theory that “the way in which CGRs are formed influences their composition and their collaboration dynamics as they evolve over time” (162). Apart from differences in formation, these CGR alternatives—classified as self-initiated, independently convened, or externally directed—also vary by “the initiating leadership, initial structure, participant volition, and group autonomy” (166). This typology is significant for both scholars and practitioners. For instance, it allows scholars to explore how a CGR’s formation might influence or color its internal dynamics, longevity, or ability to achieve specific goals. Those in a position to facilitate (or impose) collaboration can use it to think more deliberately about matching design, development, and leadership to suit particular policy or problem-solving contexts. By far, though, their strongest contribution, and likely the overwhelming ambition for the book, is their approach to assessment and accountability (thus filling a crater-sized void in our understanding of collaborative governance). Despite its prevalence as a policy-making alternative, practitioners and scholars disagree about how best to identify the “value-added” of collaborative governance regimes. For one, neither scholars nor practitioners want to impose upon collaborative governance regimes the same expectations of more top-down policy approaches, especially when, by its very nature, collaborative governance rejects hierarchical principles and practices. But by sidestepping, rather than addressing, the complexities in evaluation, we are left with little evidence to demonstrate, for instance, whether and how collaborative governance influences policy goals. This debate has immobilized would-be assessors around one basic question: Should we evaluate procedural satisfaction or, instead, should we focus on outcomes? Emerson and Nabatchi arbitrate these two perspectives and argue against this compunction to impose mutual exclusivity on the assessment options. First, they assert, collaborative governance can produce “different kinds of outcomes” to accommodate “different audiences.” But more importantly, they emphasize, “the need to assess performance from multiple perspectives” also extends to “collaborative actions and adaptations” (84). Consequently, they concede, performance measurement will be challenging. Goal multiplicity makes it difficult to develop performance rubrics; “fluid, generative, and evolving” (183) timelines create performance-scheduling headaches; and any evaluation must reflect some consensus among the diverse governing stakeholders. It is these challenges, they admit, that render collaborative governance evaluations especially susceptible to “the halo effect.” In the absence of ongoing formal evaluation, it often falls to stakeholders to offer their “post hoc perceptions” about internal dynamics and goal achievement. And although these perspectives are important, they have a tendency to be positively skewed by recent successes and diminished recollection (183). This is where their logic model is most useful. Their integrative framework is developed in part to facilitate these assessment challenges. It permits stakeholders, evaluators, scholars, or anyone interested in examining the benefits of collaboration to “trace the causal connections between inputs, processes, outputs and outcomes” (184). Individuals can use the logic model to distinguish between “process and productivity performance” (185) (which they recommend), establish temporal benchmarks, and identify interactions between structure, process, and product. In turn, researchers and evaluators can utilize the assessment tool and identify the unit of measurement, that best addresses their specific concerns. Relatedly, and equally crucial, Collaborative Governance Regimes highlights the critical linkages between conceptualization, design, and evaluation. Many readers will use the logic model simply as a way to understand and organize collaborative governance regimes. As stated above, this alone provides significant scholarly and practical import. But those who are interested (and perhaps more attuned to performance challenges) will benefit from Emerson and Nabatchi’s emphasis on the reciprocal nature of performance and design. On the one hand, design influences assessment. Before we can adequately evaluate any mode of policy-making, we need to understand how it works, how it is governed, and what it hopes to accomplish, a point that is made quite clear in Chapter 9. Without this information, any attempt to measure influence or outcomes will be at best mismatched and at worst misleading. On the other hand, assessment influences design. As many who study collaborative governance have argued, context is critical to program success. In order to effectively use collaboration as a method for resolving wicked problems, conveners must first evaluate the social, economic, geographic, and policy landscape. As Emerson and Nabatchi state “it is important to analyze this dynamic system context to develop a fuller understanding of the practicality, viability” and reach of collaborative governance regimes (40). Of course, no project, especially one as ambitious as Collaborative Governance Regimes, is without its shortcomings or caveats. First, in their effort to create a framework that is both accessible and systematic, Emerson and Nabatchi rely on concepts such as, “cross boundary collaboration,” (16) that have the potential to further complicate rather than clarify a field inundated with jargon, particularly for those who are new to collaborative governance. Second, although the book is accessible to a variety of audiences, it does require focus. This is not a book for skimming. Every section and subheading has something to contribute and if you are not paying attention you can get lost in the details. However, this is to be expected. The authors have bravely taken on the task of trying to explain a phenomenon that has developed largely as a rejection of formal rules and structures. Any attempt to organize the chaos is bound to have side effects, and the authors account for this possibility by using figures and headings to help readers locate their position within the model. Similarly, no project that attempts to raise standards and expand boundaries is immune to backlash. Devotees whose conception of collaborative governance rejects structure and rules may push back against this model. Indeed, some ideals are at risk when any phenomenon that is created to oppose institutionality and hierarchy itself becomes institutionalized. To a degree, this is what Emerson and Nabatchi have done by advancing a specific framework for collaborative governance—and encouraging conveners to adhere to a (albeit broad) set of practices and constraints. But, I think most (including those who disagree with the authors’ specific conceptions) will read this as I have—a significant, much needed, and long overdue step in the right direction.

t: Differing Goals of Limiting Autonomy: Legislatures, Governors, and State Ethics Commissions
abs: Ethics commissions address policies that are external to the policy maker, the enforcement of which may be damaging to the policymaker. Given this potential for harm it is likely that delegation to commissions is transactional with elected officials controlling autonomy based on a set of specific goals. The author tests this argument by examining how executive and legislative control of a commission’s autonomy impacts the effectiveness of a commission’s oversight. Findings suggest that elected officials attempt to influence commissions in a strategic manner based upon whether they want to direct attention away from themselves or toward the other branch of government.

t: The Relationship Between Coping and Job Performance
abs: Workers on the frontline of public service, such as teachers and social workers, cannot provide unlimited support to all their clients, because of among else scarce time and money. To deal with this, they use various coping strategies. We analyze one important coping strategy such “street-level bureaucrats” can use: prioritizing motivated clients over unmotivated clients. We study the effect of this coping strategy on job performance, as rated by their supervisors. In other words, do street-level bureaucrats who especially help motivated clients get lower or higher job performance ratings? By studying this relationship, we can test two narratives in frontline work: the state-agent narrative versus the citizen-agent narrative. If supervisors follow a state-agent narrative, they would give street-level bureaucrats that prioritize motivated clients lower performance ratings. Supervisors could stress values like legality and equality: workers should follow governmental rules and should treat all clients equally. Contrary to this, if supervisors follow a citizen-agent narrative, they would give street-level bureaucrats who especially help motivated clients higher performance ratings. Motivated clients are the “deserving clients,” worthy of investment. “Pushing” unmotivated clients may also be a very inefficient use of scarce resources. Using a multisource study of social workers in one organization in the United States, we show that supervisors give higher job performance ratings to street-level bureaucrats who prioritize motivated clients. Implications of this finding and a future research agenda are shown.

t: The Impact of Local Politics on the Principal-Agent Relationship Between Council and Manager in Municipal Government
abs: A majority of US municipalities now operate under the council-manager form of government, an institutional design that creates a principal-agent problem as the elected council and appointed manager have divergent incentives. Although current scholarship on the council-manager relationship focuses on ex post municipal level outcomes, this study advances the literature by developing a theory of ex ante contracting between principal and agent at the local level. The theory predicts that increasingly constraining political environments are associated with a greater degree of contractually provided employment protection for incoming city managers. Using unique data on California municipalities and their managers, empirical analysis supports the theory’s predictions. Specifically, as the municipal electorate becomes more cohesive and less moderate and as municipal elections become increasingly competitive, city manager contracts include increasing protection from termination in the form of severance and political protection from termination. The empirical results suggest that employment protection serves an important role in the initial creation of a principal-agent relationship between manager and council by defining the cost council must bear if they terminate the manager and protecting the manager from career risk.

t: Building Collaboration: Examining the Relationship between Collaborative Processes and Activities
abs: This study investigates if the collaborative process differs among a group of public programs involved in varying levels of interorganizational activities. Thomson and Perry (2006) suggest five process dimensions underlie collaboration: governance, administration, norms of trust, mutuality, and organizational autonomy. While these dimensions are clearly unique, it is unclear if any of these dimensions are necessary or sufficient for varying degrees of interorganizational involvement. Inventorying the interorganizational activities of pairs of government-funded preschools as ranging along a continuum of no relationship, cooperation, coordination, and collaboration, I conduct a qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) to assess the relationship between collaborative processes and activities. The findings suggest that the collaborative processes dimensions differ depending on the level of involvement. The QCA results also reveal substitutable combinations of process dimensions that underlie respective degrees of interorganizational involvement, offering insight to public managers about different skill sets they can focus on when managing interorganizational activities.

t: Motivated Reasoning about Public Performance: An Experimental Study of How Citizens Judge the Affordable Care Act
abs: Public performance reporting is often promoted as a means to better inform citizens’ judgments of public services. However, political psychology has found evidence of motivated reasoning, with citizens’ accuracy motives often supplanted by biased searching for and evaluation of information to defend prior political attitudes, beliefs or identities. We conducted a survey experiment to evaluate motivated reasoning about the performance of the US Affordable Care Act (also known as Obamacare), which has been politically contentious. In the experiment, we randomly assigned a sample of US adults to either a politics prime, to encourage partisan motivated reasoning, or a health care needs prime, to encourage accuracy motived reasoning stemming from their own perceived need for health care. We then asked them to rate the strength of real performance information in the form of evidence statements about the Affordable Care Act and to choose real performance indicators from a graphical array. The findings show that the political prime strengthened partisan differences in both the ratings of evidence statements and the selection of performance indicators. Thus, for contentious public programs where partisan identities are activated, partisan motivated reasoning influences how citizens process performance information and thus may limit its potential for enhancing democratic accountability.
