t: From High-Reliability Organizations to High-Reliability Networks: The Dynamics of Network Governance in the Face of Emergency
abs: Research has reported at length on how interorganizational networks can be effectively governed in public service delivery. In contrast, the way such networks specifically organize for reliability is strikingly absent from the literature. We substantiate the idea of High-Reliability Networks (or HRNs) by drawing from the literature on network governance and exploring networked emergency management in a large German city. Herein, we analyze an unprecedented dataset on a network’s development, covering two years of interviews and direct observations. The article offers three contributions: first, we theorize “high reliability” at the network level and thereby extend the discussion on the governance and effectiveness of interorganizational networks. Second, we show that network governance in HRNs is of a hybrid nature and oscillates between assertive and supportive modes of governance, thereby contributing to a dynamic perspective on the governance of networks. Third, the article demonstrates how HRNs develop a capacity to prepare better for the unexpected by managing latent ties.

t: Organizational Correlates of Public Service Motivation: A Meta-analysis of Two Decades of Empirical Research
abs: Public service motivation (PSM) has emerged as a central construct in the public administration literature and understanding its correlates has been a key issue. However, despite the large literature into the correlates of PSM, there is great disparity in findings, which precludes the ability to draw firm conclusions. To address this issue, we conducted a meta-analytic review of the organizational correlates of PSM. Our analysis included correlations derived from 46 studies and 48 independent samples. Results indicated that relationships estimated were generally robust to measurement method, but did vary meaningfully by national context. We also observed some evidence suggesting that PSM dimensions had distinct nomological networks. Implications of our findings are discussed.

t: The Importance of Narrative for Public Administration
abs: Narratives shape our perception, our way of thinking, and even what we do. They are everywhere in public policy, public administration, and public management, opening and constraining the possibilities for creating public value. Take for example, Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump’s recent statement: “If she [Hillary Clinton] gets to pick her judges, nothing you can do, folks…. Although the Second Amendment people—maybe there is, I don’t know” (Corasaniti and Haberman 2016). This statement alarms us not only because it presents an abhorrent idea—that gun-carrying citizens can do something to prevent a future president Clinton from nominating liberal Supreme Court justices—but also because we intuitively understand that it justifies and enables certain actions. In other words, it has (potential) causal effects. This story is rooted in and provides shorthand for a larger narrative that supports a particular identity (e.g., white male privilege), certain values (e.g., arming oneself against tyranny, authoritarianism), that is compelling for some. Other examples abound. Fracking for shale gas is narrated as an economic opportunity that will lift up struggling communities or as an environmental threat that will contribute to climate change. Within the first narrative, government agencies focus on the technological challenge of fracking: how to regulate it so as to produce the economic benefits, perhaps while also protecting the environment. Within the second narrative, agencies seek out alternative, more sustainable forms of energy and focus on figuring out how to produce enough supply to meet energy demands. While narrative approaches to research and theorizing in public administration and policy have been gaining currency for over a decade in the United States (e.g., Feldman et al. 2004; Lejano and Leong 2012; Ospina and Dodge 2005), they are still not well understood, and the unique insights they produce remain underappreciated in the broader field. David McNabb’s handbook “Research Methods in Public Administration and Nonprofit Management,” (2002) for example, covers several qualitative research traditions, but largely limits itself to those that fit within an objectivist and linear orientation to research design. This approach is appropriate for several of the qualitative traditions covered in the book (e.g., some case studies, ethnographies and action research designs), but is at odds with interpretive approaches, such as hermeneutics and semiotics (which get brief mention) and narrative inquiry (which is omitted). Sandford Borins’s recent book on narrative is a welcome addition to the field. Borins develops a framework grounded in structuralist literary theory for analyzing public sector narratives and provides in-depth illustrations of his approach in six chapters covering competing narratives of education reform in the United States (chapter 2), British governance and leadership (chapters 3 and 4), American politics and administrative decision making (chapter 5 and 6), and deliberation in American juries (chapter 7). Building on his framework, the final chapter classifies the competing narratives in each genre according to their basic narrative structure, which, in the case of governing narratives, varies on two outcome dimensions: (1) organizational renewal or organizational decline, and (2) the protagonist’s personal growth or personal decline (these dimensions would be different for other sets of narratives, e.g., of family life). The resulting two-by-two table produces six narrative types: heroic, ironic, sacrificial/retributive, and tragic/satirical. Borins’s framework makes use of Mieke Bal’s structural approach to narrative analysis in which narratives are viewed as a cultural mode of expression. From this view, narratives have several distinct features: text (words, sounds, or images composing a structured whole), fabula (character types, actions, plots, settings, and themes that can be worked into a story), story (a specific manifestation of the fabula), and polyphony (the degree to which a narrative incorporates multiple voices) (p. 6). Borins selects for analysis in each chapter a dominant narrative (the most common narrative type in a genre) and counter narratives that tend to “parody, invert, distort, or subvert” the dominant narrative, both of which provide insights on narrative content and form. Borins contextualizes his analysis of narratives with sensitivity to institutional settings, histories, and “‘real world’ issues” in which they are produced, and by relating narratives to social science theories that aid in understanding and explaining organizational and individual outcomes in the narratives. This is more or less successful in the chapters. For example, while the influence of public choice theory on public sector narratives in the United Kingdom is convincing, the use of Erik Erikson’s eight-stage model of ego development to understand and explain individual outcomes across several chapters seems to be an afterthought that does not generate particularly useful insights. Borins’s purpose seems to be three-fold: to generate context-specific and practical lessons for public managers; to support development of “narrative competence” among public management professionals, students, and analysts; and develop a framework capable of illuminating both the “managerial content of the narratives” (i.e., their central themes) and importantly their narrative structures. For Borins, narrative structures include both the formal, more general features of narrative (e.g., text, fabula and story) and the two specific outcome dimensions of governing narratives: organizational and individual growth/decline. By emphasizing narrative structures, Borins’s framework enables a comparative analysis of diverse narratives and an analysis of their narrative effects. Sound interpretive, qualitative research always goes beyond thematic description to include explanation and/or understanding (Weber’s verstehen, see Yanow and Schwartz-Shea 2014). Borins’s analysis is no exception; it uses narrative analysis to illuminate the ways narratives generate particular effects by shaping understanding and guiding action. Often, this causal property of narratives (or frames or discourses) is not well understood. A strength of the book is that it powerfully demonstrates the subjective side of governing in a highly accessible format. For instance, the chapter on the Cuban Missile Crisis contrasts a dominant narrative about President Kennedy’s extraordinary qualities as “analyzer in chief” who averts nuclear disaster by reigning in the combative impulses of his advisors with counter-narratives that give voice to a broader range of actors and perspectives, and that expose the almost accidental success of preventing the crisis and how close Kennedy came to failing. The analysis in this chapter and the others brilliantly highlights tensions and ambiguities within and across these narratives, depicting, for example, the moral ambiguity that characterizes decisions about war or the role of luck over reason in high politics. For this alone, the book will be useful for scholars in the field who want to learn about interpretive approaches to analysis and the types of insights it can generate. The book is also useful for teaching about the subjective dimensions of governing. Each of the empirical chapters could be integrated into curricula to engage students in lessons about, for instance, the political and bureaucratic uses of narrative, decision-making, deliberation, and policy change, among others. Narratives—and the analysis of narratives—convey knowledge useful for practice, in highly contextualized ways (Dodge, Ospina, and Foldy 2005). Borins takes pains to make it clear that using narrative pedagogically does not merely involve “clipping” stories from their context to highlight points about managerial skills, however useful this may be. Rather it involves training students in unpacking complex narrative structures in ways that allow for explorations of ambiguity, multiple readings, and tensions (p. 12). Like narrative research, narrative pedagogy involves going beyond the content of stories (i.e., the key themes in a text) to unpack “the mechanisms that generate the narrative effects” (p. 13), including the workings of text, fabula, and story, and the relationship these create between the author, the reader, and even social groups in society. One of Borins’s major critiques of the narrative literature in public administration, with its emphasis on narrative content, is that it largely fails to address issues of form, narrative structure and context (p. 15). Borins repeats this critique throughout his literature review for good reason; a narrow analytical focus on content guts narrative analysis such that its explanatory power is lost. Narrative content tells us little about the underlying mechanisms driving narratives and the effects they produce, while attention to structure enables such an analysis. Borins more ably demonstrates narrative competence than theorizes what it entails. His introductory chapter comes closest to defining narrative competence as “the experience of engaging critically with narrative” (p. 4), requiring skills in consuming and creating “complex and changing professional narratives” (p. 5). It seems to involve both an ability (1) to read and analyze narratives for structure and content, and (2) to create and use narratives in real time in politics and administration. The book provides more guidance on reading and analyzing narratives than creating and using them. But it could do better to conceptualize narrative competence, and to make explicit the criteria with which one judges the quality of a narrative. On the first point, there are more interesting, although implicit, descriptions of narrative competence throughout the empirical chapters. For example, the importance of empathy and “cultivated awareness of the other stories that are in play beyond one’s own” (p. 209), the importance of “develop[ing] an instinct for the narrative’s omissions and falsifications” (p. 58), the importance of using “words to express, or at least simulate, authenticity of feeling” not as spin or double speak but as astute political performance (p. 98). One of the most interesting and relevant insights is that information alone is insufficient to solve problems if it is interpreted from the perspective of the wrong narrative. As Borins puts it, narrative competence involves understanding the “blindness that comes from misreading the political narrative” (p. 131). These insights could be usefully integrated to theorize about narrative competence to demonstrate one of the most important insights of the book: that narratives have incredible power to shape perception and action. As is, these insights get somewhat lost in the details. The same could be said with respect to lessons about creating and using narratives: some ideas are provided in each chapter but the overall sense of them gets a bit lost. The final chapter attempts to bring the insights together but seems to lack a connection to the contextualized lessons in the chapters. On the second point, about judging the quality of narratives, Borins notes at several points throughout the book that some of the narratives he analyzes are of higher quality than others and provides some explanation of why this is so. But he never explicitly theorizes the quality criteria one might use to assess governing narratives (the quality of a narrative as a text, not as a research design or methodology). These criteria are likely to be found in narrative form and structure—for example, Borins does express a preference for narratives that are highly polyphonic (include multiple voices)—but largely leaves it up to the reader to piece together the particular mix of narrative features that might produce higher quality narratives. There are important implications. For example, many of the narratives that Borins analyzes are fictional accounts or documentaries that depart from the historical record or from protagonists’ real world experience. This raises questions about their truth-value and how to assess it. On one hand, this hardly matters because the point of narrative analysis is to examine narrative effects (what narratives do through their omissions and emphases) rather than how accurate they are. But on the other hand, Borins seems to suggest, we learn something when we assess a narrative’s relation to “the facts.” Borins is careful to point out that the facts are never neutral but must be interpreted, but gives us little guidance on assessing how faithfully narratives conform to “the facts,” especially when the ontological status of facts is uncertain (interpretable). Perhaps we might more usefully ask: what facts does a particular narrative support? Or which narratives allow us to act more morally? Or what is a good narrative in a polyphonic world? In each chapter, Borins offers new readings of accepted texts whose premises are largely unexamined. For example in the chapter on education reform he contrasts the dominant narrative of the heroic transformational teacher who single handedly transforms a struggling school through sheer charisma and dedication with counter narratives that demonstrate, for instance, the broader resources and skills necessary for transformation (such as planning and persuasion). The approach to narrative in this chapter is decidedly critical in the sense that it examines taken for granted assumptions and offers an alternative lens through which one might approach the transformation of struggling schools. While this is one of my favorite chapters, I find it disappointing that the lessons it draws focus on what individual teachers could do to create change rather than identifying structural changes that could be addressed. Although it does list a series of structural reform initiatives at the end of the chapter, lessons from the narratives themselves are not developed. Nonetheless, in this chapter and others we learn to read the narratives and counter-narratives and are compelled to think through their implications. What happens when we continue to uphold the individual heroic narrative? We may fail to create systems that support positive educational or other reform. This does not mean individuals do not matter but instead that they need support and resources, and skills beyond charm. Borins is careful to avoid claiming that these narratives have particular effects in the wider culture (such as influencing public opinion or bureaucratic behavior). Instead, he uses a comparative method to gain analytical purchase that enables him to draw out the emphases and omissions of each narrative and their divergent implications. Some chapters are more successful here: the first chapter convincingly shows that emphasizing the heroic transformational teachers makes us miss the important resources essential for educational reform. Single heroic teachers do not and cannot do it alone, but our dominant narrative on educational reform belies this “truth” with potentially grave consequences. In the chapters on British governance—and in the comparison between the British and American narratives—the same kinds of lessons are not as apparent. The book has other limitations. Often it presents the analyzed narratives such that readers have to rely on Borins’s representations of them, and sometimes the analysis could be more effectively done with more parsimony (e.g., chapter 5 on US political narratives). It perhaps tries to do too much, lacking a clear through line: is it a critique of the heroic leadership narrative, or is it about innovation, citizen engagement, policy change, or the politics–administration divide, or about reading narratives? But these are minor points. What comes across is Borins’s deep enjoyment in unpacking complex narratives. Each chapter in the book provides a highly compelling analysis of public sector narratives. The stories are insightful, rich, and well contextualized, providing lessons about specific public sector challenges at the individual, organizational and societal level, and about the skills required to be smart consumers and, to some extent, producers of narratives. The strength of this type of narrative analysis—its validity—is found not in its procedure but in its presentation, or in narrative terms, in its telling. Narrative analysis—along with other interpretive approaches—is particularly important for contemporary public sector research where politics and administration often involve struggle over the narrative. Who wins has far reaching consequences for policy and administrative action. We will do well to support narrative research of the type that Borins has produced in his intriguing book. It is highly relevant for teaching about and conceptualizing a prominent feature of contemporary public life.

t: What Are the Areas of Competence for Central and Local Governments? Accountability Mechanisms in Multi-Level Governance
abs: This study aims to advance understanding of the distinctive areas of competence for central and local governments. In doing so, we focus on the relative impacts of two accountability mechanisms—elections and management approaches—on the bureaucratic attitudes and behaviors exhibited within central and local governments. We posit that elections have dominant impacts in local governments, whereas management systems play a relatively larger role in the central government. Due to this difference, the central government may be better placed than local governments to administer those public service activities that either have outputs unobservable to the citizenry or require a lead time that is longer than the time between elections. This study investigates this argument empirically by taking advantage of a unique quasi-experiment in South Korea in which responsibility for administration of local water supply services changed from local governments to a central government agency. Investigating 7 years’ worth of quarterly data, we find that following the change in governance, citizen satisfaction deteriorated but efficiency improved.

Ignoring the Experts: Networks and Organizational Learning in the Public Sector
abs: Although much of the research on learning in the public sector examines collaborative arrangements and interorganizational networks, it often stresses the importance of individual dialogue and social interaction as primary methods of learning. Given the collective focus, the current emphasis on organizational interaction has left the individual mechanisms by which learning occurs unspecified and understudied. This study takes as its unit of analysis the dyadic, advice seeking ties that operate as the pathways by which knowledge is transferred and developed among organizational members. Rather than exploring a single advice or knowledge sharing network, this study offers a novel approach for examining the social dynamics of organizational learning by linking two different types of task-relevant knowledge to the social networks that emerge when employees search for that knowledge. By measuring where expertise resides in each knowledge specific network and by modeling the processes and conditions affecting knowledge transfer, this study is able to analyze how efficiently organizations tap into the resources and skills that already exist among their members. The findings suggest that employees tend to ignore the experts when seeking tacit information, and instead rely on those they feel most comfortable with and with whom are most accessible. Several important distinctions to the patterns of network formation are noted between public and private organizations. Overall, the results suggest that public managers need to pay attention to the costs of knowledge sharing as much as its benefits in order to promote organizational learning.

t: Experts, Amateurs, and Bureaucratic Influence in the American States
abs: Over the past century, the size and reach of American state governments has increased dramatically, altering the balance of power across state capitols. Although state legislatures were historically privileged as “firsts among equals,” modern administrative reforms have transformed state governments from legislative-centric to executive-dominated systems. In many states, part-time citizen legislatures now operate alongside fully professionalized executives. We introduce a new measure capturing the relative professionalism of state legislative and executive branches, allowing us to explore the policy consequences of the rising imbalance of power across states governments. Drawing upon a large panel data set of proposed and adopted state regulations from 1990 through 2010, we demonstrate that the eroding policy expertise of state legislators has resulted in increased bureaucratic participation in the policy process, as amateur politicians rely more heavily on professionalized executive agencies to define problems and develop solutions. Our findings highlight intuitive, yet understudied, consequences of common institutional reforms and speak to recent and recurring debates about the separation of powers and public policymaking.

t: Uncharted Territoriality in Coproduction: The Motivations for 311 Reporting
abs: A central question for programs that involve constituents in the coproduction of government services is: what motivates constituents to participate? This study compares two perspectives on this question: the traditional public-as-citizen model treats participation as a function of a general civic disposition that extends to many forms of civic and political participation (e.g. volunteering and voting); and we introduce the public-as-partner model, which argues that a given program might rely on any of the diverse array of human motivations, depending on the specific nature of participation required. We compare these using 311 systems, which provide a hotline and online tools for requesting nonemergency government services (e.g. graffiti removal), evaluating whether using 311 to contribute to neighborhood maintenance primarily reflects a civic disposition or is additionally motivated by a capacity for territoriality (i.e. identifying with and claiming responsibility for spaces), per the public-as-partner model. The study links three forms of information at the individual level for a sample of 311 users from Boston, Massachusetts (n = 722): objective reporting activity, derived from the 311 archive; a user survey including self-reports of civic activities and territorial motives; and voter registration records. Controlling for demographics and the contextual effects of home neighborhood, higher territorial motives predicted a greater likelihood of a person reporting any issues of public concern and reporting more issues over a broader geographical range in one’s home neighborhood (where >80% of reports are made). Civic activities and voting predicted a greater likelihood of reporting in nonhome neighborhoods (e.g. work). This dichotomy highlights the distinction between the two models in conceptualizing the motivations for participation in coproduction. The article explores how to extend this logic to the assessment of participation, outreach, and disparities in access across programs.

t: Public Service Motivation and Public Service Behaviors: Testing the Moderating Effect of Tenure
abs: Providers of public services are expected to act upon their motivation to deliver public service with the purpose of doing good for others and society (public service motivation [PSM]). While existing studies seem to support this claim, methodological shortcomings question the validity of their conclusions. We analyze the relationship between PSM and the use of home visits among Danish general medical practitioners (GPs) using a panel research design to examine how changes in PSM dimensions relate to changes in objectively measured public service behaviors. We show that GPs alter their public service behaviors according to changes in their level of self-sacrifice and compassion, as predicted by PSM theory. Importantly, we also find that behavioral effects are conditional on tenure. Longer-tenured GPs alter their public service behaviors less strongly in response to changes in their level of PSM. The findings imply that PSM is malleable and that PSM is a particular workable lever in changing public service behaviors among shorter-tenured public service providers.

t: Government Support and Charitable Donations: A Meta-Analysis of the Crowding-out Hypothesis
abs: With the growing body of literature on governance styles in which nonprofit organizations are involved in creating and implementing public services, there is a need for robust evidence on the effects of public funding on nonprofit revenues. This paper systematically reviews previous studies on the crowding-out hypothesis, which holds that private charitable donations are lower in situations of higher government support and vice versa. We find that about two-thirds of previous estimates find a negative correlation (crowding-out), while one-third of the estimates find a positive correlation (crowding-in). The results are strongly shaped by the research methods that are used. In experiments, a $1 increase in government support is associated with an average $0.64 decrease in private donations, while nonexperimental data analyses find an average increase of $0.06. Random-effects regression models show that, contrary to arguments that are prevalent in the literature, studies that take subsidies to organizations as a measure of government support are less likely to estimate crowding-out than studies that use a measure of direct government expenditures. Central government support is associated with higher charitable donations, while measures that include multiple levels of government tend to find negative correlations. The results challenge the consistency of prior research findings and demonstrate the contextual dependence of the validity of the crowding-out hypothesis.

t: The Dynamics of State and Local Contexts and Immigration Asylum Hearing Decisions
abs: Immigration judges (IJs) preside over cases related to immigration law, determining whether an individual should be granted asylum. The few prior studies of IJs have focused on factors of interest to judicial politics scholars, such as characteristics of the judge or applicant in a case. Drawing from public administration literature, we add a new set of factors related to local and state context in which the IJ works. Using multilevel regression analysis, we examine the decisions of 245 IJs made from fiscal years 2009 through 2014. Indeed, it appears context is important. We find IJs grant asylum less often in communities where citizens more often vote Republican and where the local economy is poor. Judges in states where statewide agencies have opted to participate in the restrictive immigration program 287(g) also granted significantly lower percentages of asylum applications. States with Democratic governors and state legislative majorities granted asylum more often, as do IJs working in United States-Mexico border communities. With respect to traditional factors, judges with more experience and those that hear higher percentages of cases involving individuals from Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras, grant significantly fewer petitions for asylum. Judges who hear high percentages of petitions from applicants with attorneys grant significantly more asylums.

t: Linking Network Structure to Collaborative Governance
abs: How do social networks differ between highly collaborative and less collaborative forms of governance? Drawing on a prior study that characterized the level of collaboration for three federal hydropower relicensing processes, we develop exponential random graph models of meeting attendance and participation networks. We find that the highly collaborative relicensing process had lower overall density and a propensity for relatively fewer and stronger interactions. Reciprocity is highest in the high-collaboration process, indicating that it is characterized by mutual interactions. In the low-collaboration process, patterns of connections between any three members of the network displayed a more unidirectional structure, suggesting asymmetrical interactions between active versus passive members of the network. By linking network structure to collaborative dynamics, this study helps elaborate potential mechanisms of successful collaboration.

t: The Role of Policy and Practice in Short Spells of Child Care Subsidy Participation
abs: A major change in US child care subsidy policy in 2014 established a 12-month eligibility period for families participating in the child care subsidy program. The primary policy objective of lengthening eligibility periods was to increase the stability of child care. Previous research in a small number of states has shown that families are more likely to leave the subsidy program at the time of eligibility recertification even though they may remain eligible. Using data from the state of Maryland, this article investigates whether longer eligibility periods contribute to longer continuous subsidy receipt and the degree to which local offices follow state guidelines when setting redetermination periods. Using a Cox proportional hazards model and controlling for child, family, and provider characteristics, we show that families were substantially more likely to leave the subsidy program when their voucher was due to expire or they were scheduled to recertify eligibility. We find that the span of time allotted to families before they need to recertify eligibility varied substantially across counties in ways that were not related to child or family characteristics, despite a statewide policy allowing eligibility recertification at 12-month intervals.

t: Public Sector Unions and Privatization: Evidence From the Eldercare Sector in Danish Municipalities
abs: Privatization varies considerably among local governments. One of the oft-listed explanations is the ability of public employees to block privatization. However, many studies on the influence of public employees on privatization do not use very precise measures of the influence of public employees, they have been unable to isolate a one-way effect, and the studies have not been attentive to whether the effect varies for different market forms. In this article, we focus on privatization in Denmark through a voucher market without price competition for eldercare services. Using new data for all 98 Danish municipalities in 2012, we are able to measure the strength of the public eldercare union as well as the number of the public eldercare workers relative to the number of local voters. We find that the increased union strength measured in terms of union density at the municipal level leads to substantially and significantly less privatization through the voucher market. By comparison, the estimated relationship between the relative number of public workers and privatization does not reach statistical significance. Features of the voucher market and qualitative evidence suggest that the union influence primarily goes through a direct user channel, that is through union influence directed at the service users, whereas a minor effect possibly runs through a political channel, that is lobbying directed at the local politicians.
