Neither Market Nor Hierarchy: Concurrent Sourcing in Water Public Services
abs: Analytical frameworks of government service contracting decisions typically focus on the make-or-buy decision. In concepts, governments can either produce the service itself (make) or outsource production (buy). However, governments make and buy the same public services, a practice that is termed concurrent sourcing. Drawing on transaction costs economics and the resource-based view of the firm, this article examines empirically local governments’ propensities to concurrently source public services. Using a unique data set on water public services of more than 4,500 French municipalities for four years—1998, 2001, 2004, and 2008—we find that low transaction hazards, prior contracting experience, and low production capabilities have a positive impact on the level of concurrent sourcing. These findings demonstrate that organizations’ characteristics are a significant factor in sourcing decisions and suggest that capabilities and their interactions with transaction hazards deserve heightened attention in the study of public contracting. Аналитические подходы в изучении подрядных решений в государственном обслуживании, как правило, сосредоточены на решении само-производства или закупки извне. В этих концепциях, власти либо могут предоставлять услуги сами (само-производить) или же участвовать в аутсорсинге производства (купить извне). Но, власти также могут одновременно предоставлять и закупать одни и те же общественные услуги, участвуя в практике известной под термином параллельный сорсинг. Опираясь на точки зрения из экономики транзакционных издержек и ресурсной базы в фирмах, в данной статье эмпирически рассматриваются склонности в местных органах власти к одновременному предоставлению государственных услуг. Используя уникальные данные по государственному обслуживанию в предоставлении водных коммунальных услуг в более чем 4500 французских муниципалитетах в течение четырех лет: в 1998, 2001, 2004 и 2008 годах; мы находим, что низкие транзакционные риски, предшествующий опыт заключения контрактов, а также низкие производственные возможности оказывают положительное влияние на уровень одновременных источников в предоставлении услуг. Эти результаты показывают, что организационные характеристики являются существенным фактором в поиске выбора источников услуг и говорят о том, что внутренние возможности и их взаимодействие с транзакционными рисками заслуживают повышенного внимания при изучении государственных контрактов.

t: Does Pension Plan Structure Affect Turnover Patterns?
abs: Public pension plans face pressures to cut costs. Although government costs and retiree benefits drive changes in retirement plans, policy makers should also consider impacts on turnover and retirement behavior. In the mid-1980s, Congress moved new federal employees from a traditional defined benefit (DB) pension plan to a new hybrid plan, comprised of a smaller DB plan, Social Security, and a new defined contribution (DC) plan. Early analyses of the change from the Civil Service Retirement System (CSRS) to the Federal Employees Retirement System (FERS) found a decrease in turnover rates, but our analysis of a 1% sample of federal personnel records from 1979 to 2009 indicates that exit rates for federal employees in their late 30s to early 50s are one-third higher under FERS than they were for comparable employees under CSRS. Conversions to fully DC plans by state and local governments could have even larger impacts on the stability of their workforces.

t: The Effect of Public Service Motivation and Job Level on Bureaucrats’ Preferences for Direct Policy Instruments
abs: Despite growing reliance on indirect market-based policy instruments under the New Public Management reforms, bureaucrats often prefer direct regulatory instruments. Thus, for successful implementation of indirect policy instruments, it is important to understand the underlying motives for bureaucrats’ preferences. This article shows that based on unique survey data from Korea, bureaucrats with higher public service motivation have a stronger preference for direct policy instruments. This pattern is strong for bureaucrats at lower job levels and for those who report greater willingness for self-sacrifice, but not necessarily for those who show strong commitment for the public interest. These results contradict a view that bureaucrats prefer direct policy instruments out of self-interest to maintain private benefits. Rather, direct policy instruments may require more work and even more unpleasant direct interactions with the clientele being served, but allow the bureaucrats to stay in control of and feel more responsible for the services provided.

t: Is Collaboration a Good Investment? Modeling the Link Between Funds Given to Collaborative Watershed Councils and Water Quality
abs: Collaborative environmental governance strategies seek to improve management efforts by involving nongovernmental stakeholders and spanning sectoral and geographic boundaries, but it is unclear whether government funding for such efforts efforts pays off in terms of improved environmental outcomes. This paper explores a common case of collaborative governance—collaborative watershed councils (WCs)—and examines whether the actions of collaborative WCs improve water quality. Coupling longitudinal data concerning 1984 grants given to local WCs in the state of Oregon with water quality monitoring data sampled at 161 sites, this analysis tests whether there is a prima facie case that the actions of local collaborative institutions improve environmental outcomes. Along with presenting some of the first evidence about the impacts of collaborative governance that is based on an objective outcome metric, this paper also contrasts different council actions and considers how institutional capacity impacts council efforts. WC actions are shown to be associated with improved water quality, but the magnitude of improvement is dependent on council attributes and the type of project for which funds are allocated. This paper also makes a methodological contribution by demonstrating the use of hierarchical Bayesian modeling to account for spatial and temporal dependencies present in observational data. Управление стратегий экологических общностных объединений требует улучшения управленческих усилий путем привлечения неправительственных заинтересованных сторон и охвата отраслевых и географических границ, хотя не всегда ясно окупится ли государственное финансирование таких усилий с точки зрения улучшения экологических результатов. В этой статье рассматривается достаточно общий пример управления общностными объединениями - советов по совместному управлению водоразделами (СУВ) -и исследуется связь между действиями СУВ и качеством воды. Соединив продольные данные касательно 1984 грантов, предоставленных местным СУВ в штате Орегон с данными мониторинга качества воды, собранных на 161 участках, этот анализ тестирует наличие достаточных доказательств того, что действия местных общностных объединений приводят к улучшению экологических результатов. Наряду с представлением некоторых первых свидетельств о влиянии совместного управления, используя объективное измерение результатов, в настоящей статье также противопоставляются различные действия советов и рассматривается влияние институционального потенциала на усилия советов. Показано, что действия СУВ связаны с улучшением качества воды, но величина улучшения зависит от атрибута советов и типа проектов, на которые выделяются средства. Эта статья также делает методологический вклад, демонстрируя использование иерархического байесовского моделирования для учета пространственных и временных зависимостей, присутствующих в наблюдательных данных.

t: Linking New Public Management With Public Human Resource Management Reform
abs: Public administration students in graduate programs in the United States are familiar with the tenants of New Public Management (NPM), but explaining its impact on human resources is a daunting task. Battaglio provides a great tool for teachers of human resources in the public sector. His book Public Human Resource Management: Strategies and Practices in the 21st Century successfully covers important concepts of human resources management for public administrators while centering these concepts on public human resources management (PHRM) reform, a consequence of NPM. Battaglio touches on almost all concepts related to public sector HR in his book. The book contains three parts and is divided into fourteen chapters. Chapter one is an intro to PHRM and begins part one of the book. This section then discusses the evolution of public service in the United States, employment law (with chapter three on employment law in general and chapter four focused on EEO (Equal Employment Opportunity), affirmative action, and diversity planning). Part two of the book is titled “Functions.” Like any good textbook on HR, chapters in this section discuss recruitment and selection, pay and benefits, evaluation of performance, motivation, and labor relations. The last part of the book is titled “The Future” and commences with a discussion of the privatization of HR and information systems. This section also includes chapters on strategic PHRM, PHRM education, and challenges and opportunities related to PHRM. Battaglio presents PHRM reform in chapter one and explicitly challenges common claims that the benefits of PHRM overcome its costs. After introducing five components of PHRM reform—decentralization, performance-based pay, declassification, deregulation, and privatization—he implicitly criticizes each of them. For example, describing performance-based pay (the second component of PHRM reform), Battaglio writes, “The federal government tested performance-based pay systems from 1981 to 1993 (Kellough and Nigro 2002). However, government-wide attempts during this period, which relegated performance-based pay to individual agency-level decisions, proved unsuccessful” (p. 9). As an additional illustration of Battaglio’s critical tone towards PHRM reform, he comments on its fifth component, “While the push for private sector involvement in the delivery of public services has received considerable attention in recent decades, the demonstrable evidence regarding public HRM privatization (or outsourcing) is scant” (p. 13). Battaglio does justice to the rationale for PHRM reform, reporting the logic behind the implementation of each of its five components. Nevertheless, with the possible exception of decentralization, most empirical research highlights important problems when implementing PHRM reform (p. 14). When discussing performance-based pay policies in Georgia, Battaglio notes that, “as within many states, this is often the result of the government’s desire to demonstrate legitimacy to the public—that is, while the evidence for success is sparse, the continued pursuit of accountability policies in itself is attractive to a public that feels cynical about traditional government efficiency” (p. 9). In the following chapters, Battaglio covers human resources concepts while linking the material in each chapter to PHRM reform. For example, at the end of chapter six, the reader is offered an explicit discussion of the changes brought about by PHRM reform on pay and benefits. Battaglio recommends that HR managers interested in or encouraged to try PHRM reform in pay (e.g., performance-based pay) test it on a sample before pursuing an at-large implementation. In his words, “Testing a new compensation plan as a demonstration project, to study its real-world outcomes and identify any problems, rather than implementing straightaway a system-wide overhaul will at the least save taxpayers money that would be wasted on a program that does not work as expected” (p. 177). Throughout the book, the reader is warned about the importance of following laws as well as planning for eventual challenges to existing laws. The author convinces readers of the utmost relevancy of legalism in HR by integrating disclaimers on multiple occasions in the textbook. For example, in chapter three on employment law, the author warns, “For public HR managers, careful consideration of constitutional rights is essential to avoid lawsuits. In fact, if a local government fails to take appropriate steps to train all employees in the appropriate law, the government and the HR professionals responsible for implementing training can be held liable (City of Canton v. Harris 1989)” (p. 74). This caution is made even more effective when the reader consults the appendix to the chapter. The five-line footnote recommends that “public HR managers [review] the cases in their entirety and consult with their respective legal representatives for the jurisdiction” (p. 78). The message to readers is clear: Even the author is wary of potential legal problems for himself once readers of the book begin working in HR. The textbook seeks a large audience and partially succeeds in its endeavor. A nice feature of the textbook, compared to others in the same discipline, is its laudable effort to include nonprofit organizations in the discussion on public HR. In each chapter, the reader can find a box that relates concepts to these entities. While such points might not be enough for a class full of nonprofit administrators, it works well for many courses related to public administration. These points also invite discussion in the classroom for informed comparisons of the traditional public sector (federal, state, and local governments) with nonprofit organizations. One drawback regarding the audience targeted by the textbook is found in its treatment of employment-at-will (EAW) state governments. While the book does mention EAW as part of PHRM reform or en passant, it provides no practical advice to administrators in this regime. Students intending to work in states with EAW likely need to seek additional resources beyond this textbook. Academic publications and general material on HR in EAW states are rare; more discussion on this regime would be a very welcomed addition in a future edition. A second suggestion is a more detailed treatment of sexual harassment. The book covers this issue in three paragraphs (p. 101), which does not seem to give enough importance to this topic compared to how important it is across many agencies in the United States. Overall, the central theme of PHRM reform unifies the book, and Battaglio’s tone is largely objective but also critical of the reform. I used this book in a graduate course on HR in the public sector. My students loved the book—its appearance (the summary boxes and appendices are concise and help with understanding the concepts), the fact that it was somewhat critical of PHRM (it clearly targets advanced undergrad students or grad students), the long lists of references at the end of each chapter (useful when writing research papers), and the practical case studies in chapters two through thirteen. I will reuse this textbook in my future courses. While it is not sufficient for a graduate course on its own, it is effective when complemented with additional case studies, academic articles, and presentations by eminent public HR managers.

t: JPART Virtual Issue on Citizen-State Interactions in Public Administration Research
abs: In this virtual issue, we bring together a collection of research articles that—although not usually grouped together—all illustrate the importance of citizen-state interactions. Specifically, we include articles that directly incorporate citizens’ perceptions, attitudes, experiences of, or behavior related to public administration. About 10% of all JPART articles over the life of the journal so far (1991–2015) met our inclusion criteria. Of those articles, we selected seven for this virtual issue on the basis that they have offered important insights into citizen-state interaction at different stages of the policy cycle. We argue that public administration scholarship should focus much more on the role of citizens and citizen-state interactions at all stages of the policy cycle. This research should focus both on the different forms of interaction citizens have with administrators, and the outcomes of these interactions, for bureaucracy and for citizens themselves.

t: Race and Punishment in American Prisons
abs: American prison staffs face the difficult challenge of maintaining order in an often overcrowded, potentially dangerous environment. Prison staffs are given wide discretion over treatment decisions inside prisons, including the decision to punish prisoners. Staffs are forced to make quick decisions in an uncertain environment and are likely to use commonly understood heuristics to simplify their decision-making. These heuristics include stereotypes regarding race and criminality. This article uses data on nearly 11,000 prisoners to examine the determinants of one of the harshest punishments available, the use of solitary confinement in American prisons. Consistent with the broader literature on race and criminal justice, I find that black inmates report higher rates of placement in solitary confinement than white inmates. Американские тюремные сотрудники сталкиваются с трудной задачей поддержания порядка в часто переполненной и потенциально опасной среде. Тюремным сотрудникам дана широкая свобода действий в принятии решений внутри тюрем, в том числе при принятии решений о наказании заключенных. Cотрудники вынуждены быстро принимать решения в условиях неопределенности и, скорее всего, используют широко понимаемые эвристики для упрощения принятия решений. Эти эвристики включают в себя стереотипы, касающиеся расы и преступности. В этой статье используются данные почти 11 тысяч заключенных, чтобы изучить определяющие факторы применения одного из самых суровых имеющихся в наличии наказаний - использования одиночного заключения в американских тюрьмах. В соответствии с широкой литературой по расе и уголовному правосудию, я нахожу, что черные заключенные рапортуют о более высоких долях их размещения в камерах одиночного заключения, чем белые заключенные.

t: Relative Performance Information and Perceptions of Public Service Quality: Evidence From American School Districts
abs: The publication of information about public service performance has expanded dramatically in recent decades. Multiple experiments have shown that relative performance information influences citizens’ evaluations of local services. It is unclear whether this information leads citizens to update their beliefs or temporarily employ different criteria, however, and we do not know if the influence of performance information will extend to contexts in which citizens have access to other information sources. We examine these questions using two experiments within nationally representative surveys. In the first, we find that providing respondents with information about the performance of their local schools relative to schools in the state, the nation, and other developed countries depresses average evaluations of local school quality. The second experiment shows that relative performance information depresses average evaluations in part by priming respondents to consider how the academic performance of their communities’ schools compares to others, but also by leading some respondents with erroneous prior beliefs about school performance to update their beliefs.

t: Public Sector Motivationad fonts: Personality Traits as Antecedents of the Motivation to Serve the Public Interest
abs: Public Service Motivation (PSM) is a topic that has generated considerable interest among Public Administration scholars. Research on PSM has mainly focused on either defining what PSM is and how this construct can be measured or on testing how PSM affects individual and organizational variables. However, very little is known about how the motivation to serve the public interest is influenced by personality. We evaluate the psychological antecedents of PSM by distinguishing two classes of motives behind PSM: affective versus nonaffective motives. Our analysis of data from responses to two independent questionnaires by 320 undergraduate students reveals that PSM is strongly influenced by core personality traits. Our results suggest that affective motives of PSM—Compassion (COM) and Self-Sacrifice (SS)—are positively influenced by the personality traits of Honesty-Humility, Emotionality, and Agreeableness, and negatively by Conscientiousness. In contrast, nonaffective PSM motives—Attraction to Policy-Making (APM) and Commitment to the Public Interest (CPI)—are positively associated with the Openness to Experience trait.

t: Pros and Cons of Global Governance Organizations
abs: Global governance organizations (GGOs), “a class of entities that transcend conventional dividing lines,” have integrated various stakeholder groups (e.g., governments, interest groups, civil society groups, NGOs, quasi-governmental bodies, for-profit corporations, and other concerned parties) into an increasingly integrated structure of governance (p. 295). As transnational problems rise, the need for GGOs increases. However, the underlying dynamics of GGOs have received little attention in scholarly research on governance and international relations. Based on the cases of 25 GGOs, World Rule by Jonathan G. S. Koppell examines GGOs’ struggle to maintain a balance between legitimacy and authority in different scenarios and stresses how GGOs take responses to the context-sensitive constraints. This book features nine chapters. Chapters 1–2 highlight the accountability–legitimacy tensions of GGOs. Historically, if a government is normatively legitimate, its coercive power is an essential source of authority. If it repeatedly fails to provide public services (e.g., security), this will ruin governmental legitimacy over time. As Koppell argues, in the long run, governments do not enjoy both lengthy legitimacy and authority synonymously. Attempting to balance accountability and legitimacy is a very tight rope to walk in many contexts. In most cases, such efforts end in failure. Not surprisingly, governments usually trade accountability for legitimacy, and vice versa. For example, some governments (characterized by dictatorship) are legitimate in the absence of authority while others maintain authority in the absence of legitimacy. From where Koppell sits, individuals ruled by this kind of government “do not always have the luxury of disobedience.” “Vocal objection may be the strongest response available,” because “disobedience might lead to death” (pp. 49, 67). In Chapter 3, Koppell analyzes six core characteristics—sector, rule, type, membership, funding, and technicality—that are determinants of GGO structure and process. Chapters 4–7 stress the importance of the administrative structure of GGOs (i.e., bureaucratic, centralization, and scale) and explore how interest groups participate in and influence the rulemaking process of GGOs. In many cases, governmental responsibilities will be shifted to GGOs, and GGOs will rely on governments to enforce the regulations and standards adopted by GGOs. If a government repeatedly attempts to control a GGO, this will strain resources and ultimately drive away the members of the GGO. If necessary, GGOs might grant relatively weak members necessary authority over the powerful ones. In Chapters 8 and 9, Koppell identifies three GGO models: traditional, cartel, and symbiotic. Classical GGOs are characterized by conciliar representation and centralized bureaucracy and are “associated with the forum-style rulemaking process” (pp. 300–1). Cartel GGOs are more concerned with authority than being perceived as democratic, which is associated with club rulemaking—closed and consensus-based membership. Symbiotic GGOs emphasize partnership among stakeholders and enhance compromise and implementation. As Koppell argues, “(t)he potential rule follower must calculate that adoption (and/or adherence) serves its self-interest” (p. 288). Therefore, the self-interests of concerned parties must be served. Often, concerned parties always prioritize their own interests over a more general moral calculation. As such, how should we deal with the accountability–legitimacy tensions of GGOs? In most cases, no GGO can maintain normative legitimacy while satisfying the contradictory demands of all concerned parties. To reduce the accountability–legitimacy tensions, a GGO should ensure that members’ interests will be protected. It is not surprising, then, that the outcomes of any sustainable global governance do not reduce the vested interests of key parties, though GGOs are concerned with guaranteeing the interests of less-influential members rather than authorizing the more powerful actors more privileges in rulemaking. Finally, Koppell makes reference to symbiotic GGOs—a second-best solution to the accountability–legitimacy tensions of GGOs—that ensure a minimum level of satisfaction for key stakeholders. Indeed, Koppel argues that “three-quarters of high-technology GGOs are symbiotic” (p. 307). Unfortunately, GGOs are short of enforcement powers, so it does not exclude the possibility that the most powerful member will impose their will on the GGO, meeting their own demands at the expense of other members. There are two improvements could be made to this text. First, the extent to which the arguments are applicable to the other international governance organizations, which are not stressed in this book, such as transnational security organizations, and GGOs engaging in human security. Second, as Koppell suggests, in some scenarios, the concerned parties are not motivated by profit, such as religious organizations and charities, which should be studied in future research on GGOs. Still, World Rule provides a much-needed analysis of GGOs around the world, generates good classroom debates about GGOs’ efforts in keeping a balance between accountability and legitimacy, and makes an important contribution to the growing literature of global governance, international organizations, nongovernmental organizations, and international relations.

t: Rethinking the Administrative Presidency: Trust, Intellectual Capital, and Appointee-Careerist Relations in the George W. Bush Administration
abs: How can presidents, and executives more generally, ensure the effectiveness and responsiveness of those agencies charged with implementing policy? To what is perhaps the central question in the study of public administration and the administrative presidency, many answers have been proffered, including those focused on agency design, the incentives of principals, appointee characteristics, and politicization and centralization. William G. Resh’s new—and what should soon become widely read and influential—book, Rethinking the Administrative Presidency: Trust, Intellectual Capital, and Appointee-Careerist Relations in the George W. Bush Administration, provides an additional answer to this question, clearly illustrating the importance of intra-agency trust on agency performance and its relationship with politicization. Instead of merely thinking about politicization as an attempt to influence agency policy outcomes via friendly appointments, perhaps at the cost of lowered agency performance—and blackboxing the mechanisms by how these friendlier policy outcomes are potentially reached and why agency performance is lowered—this book looks at the effect of politicization on careerists and their relationships with those appointees charged with setting the policy tone. What Resh finds in his analysis is not normatively encouraging. By starting from the assumption that politicization is undertaken because of a lack of trust on the part of the president, he makes a convincing argument that politicization engenders distrust between appointees and career executives, thereby reducing information sharing between executives and appointees, which reduces intellectual capacity and the potential for performance. In Resh’s own words: [P]oliticization negatively affects an organization’s capacity to build intellectual capital. Specifically, I propose that lack of trust becomes even more important to knowledge exchange under conditions of politicization and when appointees are trying to make things happen rather than merely stopping things from happening in order to advance a president’s policy or program agenda. Politicization diminishes the capacity to build intellectual capital because it signals distrust in careerists, especially career executives (pp. 65–6). Resh proceeds to examine this central thesis throughout the course of this impressive work, consistently finding support in a variety of contexts using a well-executed mixed-method approach. This approach works particularly well with the quantitative analysis—typically in the form of multilevel models to take into account agency-level heterogeneity—establishing general cross-level trends; qualitative interviews then provide complementary detail and nuance where necessary. The overall result is a compelling argument for the central thesis of the book. Also helpful is the way the book is organized. After outlining the previous literature on the administrative presidency in Chapter 1, Resh develops a theoretical model of trust in Chapter 2. The next three chapters are focused on empirical explorations of the implications of the theoretical model and use the aforementioned mixed-methods approach. A concluding chapter follows. Of these, I find Chapter 4 to be of the broadest interest and the one that will be most widely read (if only one is to be chosen), as it establishes the importance of intrapersonal relationships on agency outcomes. In Chapter 5, Resh delves deeper into uncovering the mechanisms by which trust affects intellectual capital, with a substantive focus on the Bush administration’s preparations for the transition of 2008–09. Though somewhat narrower in scope than Chapter 4, due to the focus on the single policy area, it is nonetheless crucial to the book’s underlying thesis. I do have some minor quibbles with the choice of policy and wish the text could have focused on another policy area in addition to the transition (in order to better determine whether the mechanism he uncovers is one that is generalizable or one that is particular to the policy area in question). This is a minor complaint, and the decision to focus on the transition was in part, I assume, due to data availability concerns. I do wish more of the text was devoted to discussing the various types of appointees and how they enhance or mitigate the relationships Resh uncovers. For example, it would be interesting to examine whether the presence of political appointees with more conventional qualifications results in higher levels of information sharing, intellectual capacity, and better performance overall relative to other types of appointees. Conversely, do “patronage” types of appointees, by virtue of their lower (on average) levels of subject-level expertise as well as the more transparently political rationales for their appointments, reduce agency performance via the same mechanism? This is particularly important because much of the recent research on agency performance has indicated that those agencies and departments led by appointees tend to have lower levels of performance (by various measures), and those led by patronage appointees tend to have the lowest levels of all (Gallo and Lewis 2012; Hollibaugh, Horton, and Lewis 2014; Lewis 2008, 2009). However, those pieces have not provided much detail outlining the actual mechanism by which these types of employees decrease agency performance. By and large, theorizing has been focused on the relative dearth of qualifications of these types of employees. Although this explanation is likely true to some extent, Resh provides a compelling complementary (or even alternative) theory to this line of research. Even though he does not address this question directly, the book does speak to it and raises questions worth examining in greater detail. One other implication of this work is the importance of work in psychology to the study of the administrative presidency. In particular, I refer to research on the psychological foundations of the propensity to trust (e.g., Matzler et al. 2008; Mooradian, Renzl, and Matzler 2006). If trust is related to information sharing, intellectual capital, and agency performance via the mechanisms outlined by Resh, then the psychological characteristics of careerists are of paramount interest. Indeed, individual-level heterogeneity in the propensity to trust others is likely to affect agency performance, and this possibility provides openings for future research. I should reiterate that these omissions should not in any way be considered to be flaws in any sense. Resh has done an impressive job of laying the foundation for what should be a productive research agenda and, above all, an important and compelling entry into the literature on the administrative presidency. As such, this text should be required reading for all scholars of bureaucracy and the administrative presidency, especially for those of the more formally inclined principal-agent orientation. Indeed, by emphasizing the importance of interactions between appointees and careerists, Resh will force those more formally inclined to begin to think of agencies less as unitary actors and more as collections of individuals. Overall, Resh has convincingly demonstrated that characteristics of individuals not only matter for agency performance but also influence the connections between these individuals, which are perhaps just as important in determining overall agency performance.

t: Less Delegated Authority Than Expected: Comparative Study on Secondary Legislation
abs: The relationship between politicians and bureaucrats remains a central theme in public policy and public administration. The breadth of theories on the subject is impressive, ranging from institutional and cultural theories emphasizing loyalty and shared goals to public choice and principal-agent models where information asymmetry predicts bureaucratic “shirking.” Empirical studies have substantiated the significant variation across time and space in the formal organization and actual practice of the relationship between elected officials and bureaucrats. Scholars disagree both on what we theoretically should expect the interactions between politicians and bureaucrats to look like and on which of the two parties is actually in charge, and why that is the case (see for instance Brehm and Gates 1997; Huber and Shipan 2002). Given this theoretical controversy and empirical diversity, sticking your toe into these infested waters might appear to be a risky enterprise. However, Edward Page is convinced that previous studies or theoretical work do not present a complete account of the interface between politics and administration. By studying secondary legislation—for example, administrative decisions on how to implement policy or apply policy to specific issues—in a comparative, cross-national framework Page seeks to shed further light on how politicians and bureaucrats interact in developing decrees. Studying the relationship between politicians and bureaucrats in processes of developing decrees in six jurisdictions—Britain, France, Germany, Sweden, the United States, and the European Union—Edward Page offers his readership a structured series of in-depth analyses of policy making in different institutional arrangements and administrative traditions. At what stages of the decision-making process are politicians or bureaucrats the lead actors, and what seems to explain differences in political and administrative involvement in the process? Page proceeds by selecting some 50 decrees that relate to a policy decision and then conducts a large number of interviews—92 in all—with bureaucrats charged with developing decrees. The selection process of decrees used for analysis is explicitly “non-random” (p. 150); decrees that appeared to be formalities with little or no policy deliberation were not included in the study. A central concern in the study is delegated authority. Such delegated authority would typically include the specification of rules on policy implementation or the application of policy on specific issues. Some degree of delegated bureaucratic responsibility is necessary for the system to work. However, delegation that is too extensive may jeopardize political oversight and accountability whereas too limited delegation might indicate that politicians spend time and resources dealing with issues that are not truly political matters. Such “secondary legislation” (p. vii) is, however, more difficult to define in practice than in theory. When does secondary legislation become de facto policy making? How is delegated authority defined and monitored in different jurisdictions? Thus, secondary legislation is ultimately a matter of striking a balance between political control and administrative efficiency. The degree of delegated authority also tells us a great deal about the level of political trust in their bureaucrats. The theoretical approach is institutional. Page argues that politico-bureaucratic relationships are shaped by recurrent interactions embedded in an entrenched system of norms and mutual expectations. Indeed, as he summarizes his findings he is dismissive of public choice theory: “the notion that bureaucrats ‘shirk’ or otherwise subvert the clear and expressed views of political leaders is based on an entirely misleading view of the nature of how public bureaucracies work” (p. 158). Page finds that politicians or agents acting on their behalf are involved in drafting decrees in about 40% of the cases. However, political involvement in the drafting of a decree does not necessarily indicate a felt need to control what the bureaucrats do. In some instances, politicians or special advisors are approached by the bureaucrats requesting a ruling on a potential political issue: “knowing that the alarm will go off anyway, bureaucrats raise it themselves” (p. 153). The relationship between politicians and bureaucrats as it is described in Page’s analysis bears very little resemblance of a principal-agent model. Instead, his account portrays their interaction as characterized by shared norms about each other’s roles, loyalty, and respect. The comparative analysis dispels several myths about the role of the bureaucracy and policy making more broadly. Thus, policy making in the purportedly “strong” French state frequently gets bogged down in complex processes of securing approval from interest groups; the British system allows for close political control, not through formal hierarchy but as an outcome of strong bureaucratic loyalty to their minister; and the “principled pragmatism” (Heclo 1987) and consensual decision making that some see as the trademark of policy making in Sweden is not a bureaucratic bargain but an accommodation at the political level, allowing for close political supervision of the development of secondary legislation. It goes without saying that it is impossible to draw any general conclusions from analyses of the processes of drafting some 50 decrees in six different jurisdictions. By the same token, the very limited number of cases precludes any general statements about the degree to which different administrative traditions or institutional arrangements differ in terms of the political involvement in developing secondary legislation. Page is very much aware of these limitations, but it was never his purpose to develop such propositions. Rather, he seeks to enhance our understanding of the specific, detailed nature of the interactions between politicians and bureaucrats. Page’s book highlights the perennial tradeoff between in-depth case studies and deductive theoretical studies. The former research strategy provides accounts of what the reality of public administration and policy making looks like; messy, contextual accounts of often complex decision-making processes fraught with ambiguity, politics, and conflict. This research strategy easily gets bogged down in detail and therefore is of little help in developing any broader understanding of the issues at stake. The latter approach, by contrast, departs from a series of assumptions about what drives agency and applies these assumptions to specific cases, either in order to formulate hypotheses or to explain the case being studied. Here, empirical inquiry—to the extent that there is any—rarely attempts to test the validity or accuracy of the fundamental assumptions but rather seeks to use empirical data to confirm those assumptions. These two research traditions have co-existed for a long period of time. Every now and then their paths cross, as happens, for instance, in Page’s analysis when he notes that his studies do not support the public choice-based notion of bureaucratic “shirking.” While one might argue that there is merit to both approaches, Page’s argument appears to be that if you want to say something profound and relevant about policy making and public administration you have little choice but to confront the richness and contradictions of the empirical world of government.

t: How Are We Doing? The Failure of Welfare Reform to Reduce Poverty
abs: The goal of Privatizing the Polity is both ambitious and important to public administration scholars. Ochs sets out to examine the extent to which public antipoverty programs since the 1996 bipartisan welfare reform have worked toward the goal of reducing poverty. Importantly, the author argues that this significant change relies extensively on the devolution of public policies to states and, subsequently, to private (both for-profit and nonprofit) corporations. As such, the success or failure of welfare reform needs to be evaluated through the complicated arrangement of public-private financing and provisions that vary significantly across the states. As such, the book will interest those concerned with how public-private contracts are managed, how well the “hollow state” implements public policies, and how effective government and private service providers are in jointly achieving goals. The book serves as an excellent overview of the alphabet soup that is the modern welfare safety net in the United States. Ochs details various public programs (TANF, SNAP, EITC, OPWDD, etc.), how these programs are intended to address poverty, and how these programs may (or may not) interact with one another. She argues persuasively that the United States addresses poverty not simply by transferring cash to those with an income below some threshold but also by managing programs intended to change certain behaviors. Further, these programs are routinely implemented not by public agencies that are held accountable (at least in theory) to officials elected by the voters but rather by private entities that may have incentives that are not consistent with public accountability. Importantly, some of these private actors are the true beneficiaries of these public programs. As an example, Ochs argues that both paternalists and neoliberal policy analysts identify the lack of a strong work ethic as one cause of poverty in many (but not all) individuals. With the problem defined as “poor work ethic,” antipoverty programs propose solutions that consist of programs intended to teach skills—both technical (hard) and interpersonal (soft)—that will permit those in poverty to successfully compete in labor markets. The book does an excellent job detailing the extent of these programs and differences between state programs. Ochs also discusses a core issue in public administration when she identifies the discretion that case workers (the public managers in this context) have in implementing the objectives of policymakers. In this context, case workers exercise discretion about who is “deserving” or “eligible” for particular programs, and this discretion is critical in understanding the effectiveness of the antipoverty program. Overall, Ochs argues that our current system does little to address the key issue of poverty. The federal government spent approximately $325 billion—about 10% of all spending—in 2012 on cash and food aid to the poor in this country, and this money flowed through 22 separate programs. This number, it should be noted, excludes other programs that might be considered public welfare by some such as health care, housing assistance, energy subsidies, etc. It is difficult not to agree a priori with this finding, given that official poverty rates have changed little between 1964 and 2012 (falling from about 19% to only 15%, with some variation during that time period); further, official poverty rates are largely unchanged since the 1996 welfare reform (US Census Bureau 2013). Poverty rates initially declined but started to steadily increase following 2000, and this trend might be consistent with the book’s theme that welfare reform aimed at changing behavior has not had a lasting effect on poverty. Interestingly, poverty has declined significantly within one particular group in the United States: those 65 and older. Many attribute this to inflation adjustments in Social Security provisions that permit the elderly to maintain purchasing power over time. More interesting, I think, is that Social Security provides cash directly to beneficiaries and does not try to alter behavior; it is more simply structured without dozens of different programs. Further, Social Security does not distinguish between the “deserving” and “undeserving.” As long as an individual has credits, benefits are determined by a mathematical formula and do not depend on managerial discretion. This is not meant to imply there are not long-term challenges facing Social Security. Instead, we can identify that the United States has a public system of cash transfers that seems to meet the goal of addressing poverty in a specific demographic. Although poverty rates have fallen among those 65 and older, those most likely to be in poverty are young, single-earner households, and people of color (relative to the general population). This does seem to lend some credence to Ochs’s argument that public attempts to alter behavior have not worked. As a result, poverty rates have increased, and these populations are increasingly alienated from the system that theoretically exists to aid them. Although the book will serve future researchers well for its documentation of the antipoverty programs, the book’s primary finding—that neoliberal and paternalist programs have not reduced impoverishment—is drawn from a statistical model that is not entirely convincing. The model uses state-level data from 1990 to 2008 to analyze how different policies and mechanisms affect rates of impoverishment. A panel of this length would seem, at a minimum, to be served well by state fixed effects or a first-difference model to minimize potential omitted variable bias. Absent these, it is difficult to place much weight in the results because the estimated coefficients may not be accurately estimated. For example, the current model does not include such variables as change in employment by industries or change in population; both could theoretically influence the impoverishment level of a state’s population. If very poor citizens move out of a state, for example, impoverishment would likely change. Similarly, if high-wage industries move out while low-wage industries move in, the level of impoverishment will also change. In a similar vein, it is never made clear why certain demographic or policy variables are lagged and others are not. For example, it seems reasonable that unemployment rates might influence impoverishment with a lag—because unemployment benefits take time to expire. Welfare caseloads may also be lagged, if for no other reason than to ensure reverse causality is not biasing the results. After all, although welfare caseloads may influence impoverishment, does impoverishment also influence welfare caseloads? Further, I would prefer to see more direct interpretation of the model’s output. For example, the mean impoverishment score in the sample is 31.62. States that have enacted workfare policies in which welfare recipients must enter the workforce to receive benefits are associated with a 0.06 unit increase in impoverishment. Rather than suggesting that workfare increases impoverishment, it seems a better interpretation is that workfare has no meaningful effect on impoverishment, even if the result is statistically significant. The problem, however, is that advocates of workfare may argue that the policy is not really hurting on average. Drilling deeper into states’ experiences with workfare policies would allow us to examine which states had programs that meaningfully reduced impoverishment or were more effective than others. Framing her discussion in the limitations of neoliberalism and paternalism, Ochs finds that current antipoverty programs fail those individuals it purports to help and instead aids private actors. I also wonder if this failure is related to even larger issues beyond the goals of welfare reform. We have a system of government that was originally conceived as a mechanism to ensure and protect negative rights (not entirely, but predominantly) and does a fairly good job in this task. As society has moved to enshrine positive rights, including antipoverty economic rights, we should not only question the embedded theories or values as Ochs has done in this book but we may also have to consider that our government and bureaucracy were largely established to refrain from action. We now are asking them to act, and the results are unsatisfactory. Would we see different results from our “War on Poverty” if we provided cash assistance, minimized behavioral “nudges” to move people toward preferred actions, and let recipients spend their time as they choose rather than trying to navigate the modern welfare bureaucracy? Finland, by way of example, recently scrapped its welfare system and provides all citizens with cash payments. Comparative analysts of welfare policies and public administration should follow this experiment to determine whether it has more effective results than the one it replaced. Although I do not find the empirical support for her conclusions absolutely convincing, Ochs does make a compelling case that the US system is not meeting the goals established for welfare programs. The beneficiaries of these programs are not the poor, and a tremendous amount of public dollars are inefficiently expended as a result. Future experimental research might expand our limited understanding of guaranteed income programs as replacements for our current morass of welfare programs to provide more protection from poverty and impoverishment. Basic income support, it seems, might make antipoverty programs effective again.

t: Disentangling the Causal Mechanisms of Representative Bureaucracy: Evidence From Assignment of Students to Gifted Programs
abs: Scholars have suggested that the benefits of representative bureaucracy arise from bureaucrats acting in the interests of clients who share their characteristics, increased diversity encouraging even nonminority bureaucrats work to further the interests of minority clients, and/or the actions of clients that are more responsive to bureaucrats that share their characteristics. Despite decades of research, the literature has been unable to empirically disentangle these mechanisms, primarily because the vast majority of studies examine only organization-level data, and, at the aggregate level, they all produce identical findings. In contrast, this study makes use of data that allows us to observe the behavior of individual clients and bureaucrats, as well as the aggregate characteristics of the organizations in which they interact. Specifically, we make use of student-level data to predict differences in the probability that an elementary student is referred to gifted services by race. Our results suggest that black students are more likely to be referred to gifted services when taught by a black teacher but that increased presence of black teachers in the school other than the classroom teacher has little effect. We find some evidence that the classroom teacher effect is partially driven by teachers’ more positive views of own-race students. Our results do not suggest, however, that the positive impact of teacher-student race congruence on gifted assignment can be explained by differences in student test score performance or increased parental interaction with the teacher. Ученые предпологают, что выгоды от представительной бюрократии возникают из чиновников, действующих в интересах клиентов, которые разделяют их характеристики, из увеличения разнообразия среди сотрудников, которое поощряет даже чиновников не являющихся членами меньшинств к продвижению интересов меньшинств, либо из действий клиентов, которые более открыты к бюрократам разделяющим их характеристики. Несмотря на десятилетия исследований, литература не смогла эмпирически распутать эти механизмы, в первую очередь потому, что подавляющее большинство исследований рассматривает данные только на уровне организации, где на агрегированном уровне, все исследования производят одинаковые результаты. В отличие от этого, это исследование использует данные позволяющие нам наблюдать за поведением отдельных клиентов и чиновников в совокупности с характеристиками организаций, в которых они взаимодействуют. В частности, мы используем данные на ученическом уровне для предсказания различий в вероятности того, что ученик начальных классов направлен на услуги для одаренных детей по признаку расы. Наши результаты свидетельствуют о том, что черные ученики имеют больше шансов быть отнесены к услугам для одаренных, когда учитель является черным, но, что увеличение присутствия черных учителей в школе, кроме учителя в классе мало на что влияет. Мы нашли доказательства того, что эффект классного учителя частично зависит от более позитивных взглядов учителя об учениках собственной расы. Наши результаты не показывают, однако, что позитивное влияние конгруэнции расы между учителем и учеником на запись к услугам для одаренных можно объяснить различиями в баллах на ученических тестах или повышениями родительского взаимодействия с учителем.

t: Public, Nonprofit, and For-Profit Sector Regulatory Approaches in Third-Party Regulatory Administration
abs: Many contemporary regulatory programs rely on third-party organizations to fulfill monitoring and enforcement functions. Third-party regulatory designs introduce complexity and potentially conflicting incentives that can impact program delivery. This article examines how regulatory program outputs are shaped by third-party administrators through an investigation of the organizations charged with administering US organic food regulations. Based on the notion that third-party arrangements draw attention to administrator organizational characteristics, the article asks: To what extent does sector (public, nonprofit, for-profit) affect third-party administrators’ regulatory approaches in the administration of uniform regulatory standards? A secondary analysis explores an economic facet of dimensional publicness among nonprofit third-party administrators. The study draws on regulatee survey data and uses multilevel analysis to account for how regulatory approaches vary across third-party administrator characteristics, as well as according to respondent-level attributes. The findings indicate that little systematic variation in regulatory approaches can be attributed to administrator sector. The facet of regulatory approach in which sector appears to play a role is found in public third-party regulatory organizations’ lower provision of technical assistance, when compared to their for-profit counterparts. The article discusses explanations for the limited relationship between third-party sector and regulatory approaches and suggests future research for better understanding the linkage between regulatory program design, administrator organizational characteristics, and program outputs. Многие современные регулятивные программы зависят от сторонних организаций для выполнения функций мониторинга и правоприменения. Нормативные конструкции использующие третье-сторонние организации вносят элемент сложности и стимулируют потенциальные конфликты, которые могут повлиять на осуществление программ. Данная статья рассматривает как формируются результаты регулятивных программ сторонними администраторами на примере изучения организаций, которым поручено управление правилами производства органических пищевых продуктов в США. Основываясь на том, что сторонние механизмы привлекают внимание к организационным характеристикам администратора, вопрос в статье гласит: В какой степени сектор (т.к. государственный, некоммерческий, или коммерческий) влияет на подходы третье-сторонних администраторов в правовых подходах к управлению едиными регулятивными стандартами? Вторичный анализ исследует экономический аспект размерности в уровне публичности среди некоммерческих сторонних администраторов. Исследование основано на данных опроса среди регулируемых лиц путем использования многоуровневого анализа для учета того как регулятивные подходы отличаются по характеристикам сторонних администраторов, а также в соответствии с атрибутами на индивидуальном уровне. Полученные данные свидетельствуют о том, что сектор администратора связан с меньшим уровнем систематических вариаций в регулятивных подходах. Аспект в регулятивном подходе, где сектор играет роль связан с тем, что государственные сторонние регулятивные организации предлагают меньше технической помощи, по сравнению с коммерческими эквивалентами. В статье обсуждаются причины отсутствия связи между сектором сторонних организаций и их регулятивными подходами, а так же предполагаются дальнейшие вопросы для будущих исследований для лучшего изучения связи между дизайном регулятивных программ, организационными характеристиками администратора и программными итогами.

t: Dispersed vs. Centralized Policy Governance: The Case of State Early Care and Education Policy
abs: Policy and public management scholars have long theorized about the fragmentation of policy governance across numerous agencies, yet the effects of concentrated or dispersed governance on outcomes of the target population are largely unknown. Child policy is a policy field where dispersion has raised particular concerns, leading several states to consolidate governance for children’s programs in recent years. After presenting arguments both for and against the dispersion of policies across agencies, we estimate the effect of dispersion of state-level early childhood education policy governance on children’s reading skills. Using a unique nationally representative, longitudinal data set of young children merged with rich state-level data, we use instrumental variables estimation to address potential endogeneity of state governance policies. Our findings indicate that there is a significant positive effect of dispersed governance on children’s reading skills in kindergarten. The returns to dispersion diminish above four agencies. Future research in this area should explore the specific mechanisms through which policy governance affects child outcomes. Ученые в области политики и государственного управления давно теоретизируют о фрагментации в управлении политикой во многочисленных агентствах, но результаты концентрированного либо рассредоточенного управления на последствия среди целевых групп внутри населения в значительной степени неизвестны. Политика по уходу за детьми представляет собой поле действия, где дисперсия вызывает особую озабоченность, что в некоторых штатах в последние годы привело к консолидации управления детскими программами. После представления аргументов за и против дисперсии политики внутри государственных агентств на уровне штатов, мы оцениваем влияние дисперсии управления политикой образования во время раннего детства на навыки чтения среди детей. Используя уникальный, репрезентативный в масштабе всей страны набор продольных данных о детях младшего возраста, объединеных с богатыми данными на уровне штатов, мы используем метод исчисления инструментальных переменных, который устраняет потенциальную эндогенность в управлении политикой в штатах. Полученные нами данные свидетельствуют о том, что существует значительный положительный эффект дисперсного управления на навыки чтения среди детей в начальном классе. Возврат от дисперсии теряется выше четырех учреждений. Дальнейшим исследованиям в этой области следует изучить конкретные механизмы, посредством которых политика управления влияет на результаты среди детей.

t: Clerks or Kings? Partisan Alignment and Delegation to the US Bureaucracy
abs: Scholars often assert that the delegation of policy discretion to administrative agencies is driven, in part, by partisanship. In short, the “ally principle” dictates that elected officials delegate more policy discretion to agency officials when their partisanship aligns because such an alignment reduces uncertainty about future policy choices. In contrast, we draw on insights from social identity theory to theorize that partisan alignment may, in practice, decrease the overall perceived policy discretion by agency officials. We evaluate this hypothesis using data collected across three decades of state political elections and over 6,000 American state agency heads, finding consistent evidence against the ally principle. In fact, in keeping with our theorizing, we uncover slightly lower—not higher—levels of policy discretion are associated with partisan alignment. We conclude that partisanship may play a role in narrowing the perceived policy authority available to politically like-minded agency officials. Ученые часто утверждают, что административным органам делегируют свободу действия в выборе политики, в частности, по причине партийного выравнивания. Вкратце, «принцип союзника» диктует, что выборные должностные лица делегируют больше свобод в выборе политики должностным лицам государственных агентств, когда их партийная принадлежность выравнивается, так как такой расклад уменьшает уровень неопределенности в отношении политического выбора в будущем. В противоположность этому, мы опираемся на идеи из теории социальной идентичности и теоретизируем, что, на практике, партийное выравнивание может в целом уменьшить восприятие среди чиновников государственных агентств об уровне делегированных полномочий. Мы оцениваем эту гипотезу, используя данные политических выборов собранных в течении трех десятилетий на более чем 6000 руководителей структур на уровне Американских штатов, и находим убедительные доказательства против принципа союзника. На самом деле, в соответствии с нашей теорией, мы раскрыли не больший, а меньший уровень делегирования полномочий в случае партийного выравнивания. Мы пришли к выводу, что партийное выравнивание может играть определенную роль в сужении воспринимаемого политическими единомышленниками-чиновниками из государственных агентств об уровне предоставленных им полномочий.

A Systems Theory Approach to Innovation Implementation: Why Organizational Location Matters
abs: In this study, we evaluate the “success” of adopted innovations in public organizations as a function of the relative source of innovation vis-à-vis the organizational environment. We argue that the source of innovation will be varyingly associated with subsequent perceptions of implementation success depending on locational characteristics of the source and the innovation’s outcome locus. Neither “top-down” nor “bottom-up” arguments of implementation offer a complete picture of perceived implementation success of public sector innovations. Rather, in addition to the vertical perspective (“top-down versus bottom-up”) of implementation success, it is the relative proximity the source has to the related process or result that matters, which is represented by a horizontal perspective (organization’s core versus organizational boundary or external environment). Our empirical results offer evidence that this expected configuration of relationships, consisting of both vertical and horizontal perspectives simultaneously, indeed exists in the public sector. В данном исследовании мы оцениваем «успех» принятых инноваций в общественных организациях как функцию от относительного источника инноваций по отношению к организационной среде. Мы утверждаем, что источник инновации связан с последующим восприятием его успеха, в зависимости от характеристики местоположения источника и его конечного локуса. Ни аргументы объясняющие реализацию проектов по схеме "сверху-вниз", ни по схеме "снизу-вверх" не могут предложить полную картину восприятий успешного внедрения инноваций в государственном секторе. Скорее всего, в дополнение к вертикальной перспективе («сверху-вниз против снизу-вверх») успеха реализации инноваций, значение имеет относительная близость источника к соответствующему процессу или результату, что представлено в горизонтальной перспективе (от организационного ядра к организационной границе или внешней среде). Наши эмпирические результаты свидетельствуют, что такая ожидаемая конфигурация отношений, состоящая одновременно из вертикальных и горизонтальных точек зрения, на самом деле существует в государственном секторе.

t: Public Service Motivation and Sense of Community Responsibility: Comparing Two Motivational Constructs in Understanding Leadership Within Community Collaboratives
abs: Leadership has been recognized as one of the most critical elements to successful community collaboration. However, to date, we have limited knowledge of what drives people to embrace voluntary leadership roles. In this study, we investigate the intersection and relative contributions of two “other-regarding” motivational constructs in predicting peer nominations of leadership in community collaboratives: public service motivation (PSM) and psychological sense of community responsibility (SOC-R). In doing so, we aim to both introduce a new construct (SOC-R) to the field of public management as well as clarify the theoretical relationship of PSM and SOC-R to each other as well as to indicators of collaborative leadership. Study findings indicate that while SOC-R was significantly related to being identified as thought leaders and champions of a collaborative, PSM has no significant direct relationship to either indicator of collaborative leadership. However, PSM was significantly and positively related to SOC-R and was shown to have a significant indirect effect on indicators of collaborative leadership. These findings contribute to a growing literature seeking to clarify the role of PSM in understanding organizational behavior. Findings further suggest that SOC-R is a promising construct for understanding prosocial organizational actions such as collaborative leadership. These findings have significant implications for both advancing theories of motivation in public service-oriented contexts and their relationship to leadership behaviors. Лидерство признано одним из наиболее важных элементов для успешного сотрудничества в рамках общностных объединений. Тем не менее, на сегодняшний день мы имеем ограниченные знания о том, что заставляет людей принять добровольные руководящие роли. В данной работе мы исследуем пересечение и относительный вклад двух мотивационных конструкций связанных с заботой "о других" в прогнозировании номинаций сверстников на лидерские позиции в общественных объединениях: мотивация служения обществу (PSM) и психологическое чувство ответственности к общности (SOC-R). При этом мы стремимся ввести новую конструкцию (SOC-R) в область государственного управления, уточнить теоретическую взаимосвязь между PSM и SOC-R, а также уточнить их связь с индикаторами совместного лидерства. Результаты исследования показывают, что в то время как конструкция SOC-R в значительной степени связана с такими идентификациями как «лидер мышления» и «чемпион совместного объединения», PSM не имеет существенного прямого отношения ни к одному из этих индикаторов совместного лидерства. Однако конструкция PSM существенно и положительно связанна с SOC-R и было показано, что она оказывает существенное косвенное влияние на индикаторы совместного лидерства. Эти выводы привносят вклад в растущую литературу, которая стремится выяснить роль PSM в понимании организационного поведения. Полученные данные позволяют предположить, что конструкция SOC-R является перспективной для понимания просоциальных организационных действий, таких действий как совместное лидерство. Эти выводы дают серьезную причину для продвижения обеих мотивационных теорий в контексте служения обществу, а также их причастности к лидерскому поведению.

t: Agency Structure and the Distribution of Federal Spending
abs: Agency structure can shape agency independence in two ways. First, it can insulate agencies from policy demands from political overseers in Congress and the executive branch. Second, agency structure can shape the range of available options from which agencies can select policy. In this article, we present a novel empirical approach that evaluates both types of effects by modeling the mean and variance of agencies’ policy decisions. Analyses of US distributive program spending across 10 congresses and 68 federal agencies show that agencies structured for independence enjoy a broader range of options from which to implement policy but are no less responsive to spending demands from members of Congress and the president.

t: How Leaders Respond to Diversity: The Moderating Role of Organizational Culture on Performance Information Use
abs: Two central governance challenges are directing leadership attention to performance data and the management of diversity. This article examines connections between the two, asking if the introduction of diversity, as a form of organizational change, is associated with greater leadership use of performance data. Diversity is theorized as a double-edged sword for organizations, generating greater innovation, creativity, and performance, but also conflict. We propose that leaders will be motivated to use performance data to understand, manage, and explain the effects of diversity. To study this question, we employ a randomized controlled field experiment where organizations are assigned new employees that bring role and educational diversity. We find that leaders are more responsive to these two types of functional diversity when they view their organization as lacking an innovative organizational culture.
