The Lagged Effects of Job Demands and Resources on Organizational Commitment in Federal Government Agencies: A Multi-Level Analysis
abs: Based on the Job Demands-Resources literature and social exchange theory, this study examines the lagged effects of job resources and job demands at the agency level on organizational commitment at the individual level, with these effects mediated by individual-level demands and resources. Using hierarchical linear modeling to analyze data obtained from federal government employees (agency N = 38, employee N = 295,851), this study found that aggregated job resources (empowerment, cooperation, feedback) were related to higher employee commitment over time, with this effect mediated by lower levels of perceived workload. Furthermore, aggregated workload was negatively related to commitment over time, with this effect mediated by lower levels of perceived job resources. This study provides further empirical evidence for the lagged effect of job resources and job demands in predicting employee commitment. Furthermore, this study found interrelations among demands and resources across levels of analysis, addressing theoretical relationships that have remained largely unexamined in the context of job attitudes and commitment research.

t: Public Administration Theories: Instrumental and Value Rationality
abs: This book analyzes eight families of public administration theories from the perspective of instrumental and value-based rationalities. In the category of instrumental rationality, Dong places Traditional Public Administration, Privatization, New Public Management (NPM), and Holistic Governance. In the value-based camp, we find New Public Administration, Democratic Administration, New Public Service, and Public Value Management. The eight theories are analyzed along five additional dimensions: core value, human nature, methodology, rule of government, and disciplinary position. The author describes the historical trajectories of the two schools of thought over the last century and presents a new perspective on theoretical development. He proposes a complex evolution of public administration theory and claims that there have been pendulum movements between instrumental and value rationality over time. This book’s strength lies in classifying and analyzing different public administration theories. The author has a very good command of different theoretical traditions, and he makes a systematic analysis along many meaningful dimensions. One could ask whether these eight theories are mutually exclusive or whether they partial overlap. One example occurs with Privatization and NPM; for many scholars, privatization is a prominent component of NPM reforms. One can also wonder if they are exhaustive. I miss, for example, the institutional turn in public administration ( March and Olsen 1989 ), the neo-Weberian reform trends ( Pollitt and Bouckaert 2011 ), or the growing research on public sector motivation ( Perry and Hondegem 2008 ). Another concern is whether these eight theories really are coherent and consistent or broad and loosely connected theoretical ideas under different umbrellas. For example, NPM is not based on a coherent theory but is a mixture of economic organization theory such as principal agent approaches and management theories such as the managerialism turn in public administration. While the first is based on solving the mistrust between the principal and the agent through incentives, contracts and centralization management theory is based on trust and openness for delegation, flexibility, and autonomy for subordinate bodies. Further tension exists where NPM prescribes both centralization and decentralization. It is also a bit ambiguous what the difference is between different public administration theories and different administrative reform trends and trajectories. More generally, one could ask if we really have any generally accepted theory in public administration that specifies the conditions in which one set of factors have greater explanatory power than others or how the mutual influence of different predictors can be understood ( Olsen 2007 ). I also wonder how fruitful the stage approach is in this text. Reading this book, one gets the impression that new theoretical approaches replace previous approaches over time. I think it is more fruitful to look at the different approaches as complementary or supplementary perspectives. My argument is that public administration is a composite system in which one has to find a balance between competing goals and values ( Olsen 2010 ). There are lasting and permanent tensions between hierarchies, markets, and networks. Important trade-offs are constantly made between loyalty to political principals, Rechtsstate values, stakeholder interests, and more. In my view, the pendulum metaphor does not capture the complex and hybrid nature of public administration. What we have witnessed over the past decades is not a successive replacement of one model by another but rather a complex process of adaptation and layering, leading to the coexistence of multiple doctrines. A separate concern is that this text has a strong US bias; it is mainly about US exceptionalism in public administration research. Somewhat surprising is that it does not link to the old Chinese Confucian tradition ( Hood and Jackson 1991 ) or to the rather rich European tradition ( Pollitt and Bouckaert 2011 ). Except for Max Weber, prominent contemporary European scholars like Christopher Hood and Christopher Pollitt are only briefly mentioned, and works by Walter Kickert (on comparing the European and American traditions) and B. Guy Peters are overlooked. In general, the opportunity for a stronger comparative approach in this book is missed. Theoretically, it is also unfortunate that the institutional turn in public administration research is more or less ignored (such as work by Olsen and March, Brunsson, and others). It is a bit surprising that the work by Philippe Seltznick is not mentioned given the strong focus on value rationality and the importance of culture. One interesting debate that is briefly addressed in this book is the question of whether public administration is a stand-alone discipline or a subdiscipline of political science. Perhaps the Scandinavian take on the study of public administration as mixture of political science and organization theory with a substantial empirical orientation is a fruitful combination. These features were typical in public administration research in United States until 1960 but have since fallen out of favor ( March 1997 ). One point that is not discussed in the book is the empirical support that exists for each of the theories. Do these work in practice? For example, will NPM lead to a government that works better and costs less as promised? Unfortunately, there is still very little evidence on the effects, for example, of privatization and NPM. One exception is the book by Hood and Dixon (2015) ; the authors conclude that in the United Kingdom, NPM has led to a government that costs a bit more and works a bit worse. What the discipline probably needs more than anything else is good comparative data both over time and across countries. The book could also benefit from a discussion about the generic catch-all macro-oriented theories versus meso-level theories that take contextual constrains into consideration ( Pollitt 2013 ). In my view, we have to go beyond generic theories that can be applied everywhere, at all times and in all situations. Instead, we should go for institutional theories that take contextual constraints into consideration. For example, it will make a big difference if an agency is working in a society where the citizens have low trust in government institutions (such as the United States) compared to an agency operating in a high trust society (such as Scandinavia). The same can also be said for high corruption versus a low corruption contexts ( Holmberg and Rothstein 2012 ). There is also a need for public administration to go back to its roots to address the big issues that contemporary political systems have to deal with such as climate change, migration, demographic and technological changes, and security. We have to go beyond the internal management problems and address the wicked issues that societies are currently facing in explaining the path of administration ( Roberts 2014 ). This is an issue throughout public administration as a discipline, but it is not given much attention in this book. In sum, reading Dong’s stimulating book evokes some critical thoughts about the role of public administration theories in contemporary governance systems. Dong has written a comprehensive book with an innovative take on different theories. He points rightly to the importance of the traditions of public administration theories, and the book give new insight to the trajectories of these theories and the complexity of instrumental and value-based rationality. Still, it does not give readers a full answer.

t: Review ofAdvanced Introduction to Public Policyby B. Guy Peters
abs: Introductory textbooks for public policy must strike a balance between academic, theory-driven work and the practitioner-oriented, real world of public policy. Academics are increasingly asked to explain how their theories explain policy, and practitioners often look to scholars to understand how observed policy problems contain common theoretical elements. Peters addresses both of these audiences in Advanced Introduction to Public Policy. Within the text, Peters explains theoretical perspectives of the policy process while also providing many relevant applications of policy concepts for students of public policy. Notably, he achieves this in 10 concise chapters that do not become overly burdensome to the reader. Throughout the text, Peters offers a detailed account of public policy from the “design perspective,” specifically working with three components of public policy design: causation, intervention, and evaluation. These three elements provide a broad outline for the book. Overall, the design perspective offers a relatively new and approachable way for policy students to understand the multidimensional field of public policy. The two introductory chapters provide an explanation of his meaning of the design perspective and what this approach offers to the policy dialogue. The motivation for studying policy design is that it offers a more holistic view of the policy process, especially the linkages between causation, intervention, and evaluation. The design perspective also gives more attention to the development of policy interventions rather than traditional examinations of policy analysis. In these introductory chapters, the discussion of design is enriched by the examination of policy evolution, rationality, risk, and the role of the public sector and nongovernmental actors. Furthermore, Peters draws on a multidisciplinary perspective, tapping fields of public policy, public administration, political science, economics, law, sociology, and ethics to describe the policy process. Peters also provides basic explanations of why the private market fails and, thus, society needs public policy. Special attention is given to defining and characterizing policy problems. After the introduction to the study of public policy, the book is segmented into three parts for an in-depth examination of each of the elements of policy design. Part I (two chapters) unpacks causation by discussing several theoretical models of policy making and agenda setting. Rationality, bounded rationality, institutional analysis and development, multiple streams, issue attention cycle, politics of agendas, and many other theories are discussed throughout these chapters. Although the text does provide explanations on some of the classic theoretical models every student of public policy should be aware of, it is not a complete substitute for other policy theory books. The theoretical models in this text are but a brief introduction to motivate the portion causation of the design perspective. Overall, this section offers a balanced discussion of the practical sense of policy theory and the major theoretical research questions. This section of the book is not overwhelmed with citations to scholarly work on each of the theoretical models. However, elaborating on practical applications of theory, this section becomes more meaningful for the practitioner-oriented student. Part II details the intervention component of policy design. In the two chapters devoted to this element, Peters examines the instruments used during policy implementation; this includes the designing and structuring of implementation; promoting compliance among bureaucrats, citizens, and elected officials; and successfully evaluating implementation. Peters devotes significant space to elaborating on classifying, choosing, and evaluating instruments. As is common of this text, both chapters are well explained with current policy illustrations. An analysis of evaluation is provided across three chapters in Part III of the text. Peters considers different types of methods to assess the success of policy, explaining the advantages and disadvantages of each. Furthermore, Peters addresses both how to evaluate the efficiency and effectiveness of a policy as well as how to assess the normative and ethical dimensions of the policy. This is perhaps the best contribution of the book; unlike many other introductory policy texts, Peters gives a thorough consideration of the ethical and normative implications of policy. These are important factors that administrators must consider in their evaluations, yet they often get overlooked because of “bottom line” dollar amounts pressures to maximize efficiency. The final chapter offers an overview of the design perspective. In addition, Peters discusses how to identify policy success as opposed to more easily recognizable policy failure. Assessing policy success and failure can be a highly contentious process that has many dimensions. Peters’ discussion of Affordable Care Act provides a clear and articulate illustration of the fact that there are many points of view as to whether a policy is seen as a success or failure. One of the many advantages of this book is that it is concisely written and well organized. It is smaller than the average introductory public policy book at about 200 pages. Even accounting for the smaller size, it is important to emphasize that this is an advanced introductory book. It may serve best for graduate courses with a heavy emphasis on group discussions. The book does not lend itself well to undergraduate lecture courses since chapters do not contain simple, convenient bullet points of chapter objectives. Each chapter is densely written with a wealth of material that gives the reader much to think about and discuss and not necessarily a list of things to memorize. Reading this book should provoke thoughts related to policy applications that lead to fruitful class discussions. Furthermore, this book offers a plethora of real-life policy examples that make theoretical concepts more manageable and easy to grasp. Examples cover a wide range of topics from health to education and other types of policy. Given that emphasis, it makes the book appropriate for both practitioner and academic audiences.
